output:
*Mireille counts on her fingers as she looks around the small dwelling*

"Four mouths, 360 for upkeep, 120 for the tax... that's 480 out before I even step out the door, you understand?" *she mutters, scratching her chin*

*She turns to her household, her voice warm but carrying that undertone of worry that always creeps in when she counts money*

"Kenji, Esme, Ezra - I'm off to meet the crew. Giselle's probably already pacing at the site wondering where her hands are. I'll bring back what I can."

*She smooths her work clothes and makes a quick mental note - she needs to check if there's any food in the house the children can eat, but more importantly, she needs to get to work and start earning. The construction company is where the sim comes from to keep this household running.*  *Mireille steps into the construction yard, the familiar smell of sawdust and stone dust greeting her like an old friend. She spots Giselle already there, probably reviewing the day's plans, and Arjun who she's worked plenty of jobs with before.*

"Morning, Giselle. Arjun." *She gives them both that easy grin that makes folks feel like they've known her for years.* "What's the word for today, you understand? Where are we putting our backs into?"

*She counts off on her fingers as she speaks, habits that die hard* "Four for upkeep, one-twenty for the tax... need to make sure we're solid today, boss."

*She casts a sideways glance at Giselle - they've worked together long enough that Mireille knows the other woman carries the weight of keeping the company afloat, same way Mireille carries the weight of her household. Same weight, different shape, you understand?* *The morning's started already. She stands with her coworkers, waiting to hear what Giselle's got planned for the crew. Construction work - honest labor for honest sim. The paperwork can wait, but the building won't, you understand?*

*counts on fingers* Four mouths, one-twenty for tax, forty for shelter, thirty for heat... that's two-eighty before we've even put a grain in anyone's belly, you understand.

*looks around at the crew gathered, gives a slow nod to Idris as he arrives*

"Morning, Idris. You didn't miss much yet—Giselle's still sorting out where she needs us most. Though with five of us standing here counting on today's wages, I'm hoping there's enough foundation left to go around."  *turns attention to Giselle, fingers still half-curled from counting*

"You've got the crew assembled, Giselle. Five backs, five hammers, five families waiting on what we earn. What's the job? You understand—I'm not one for standing around when there's stone to be moved and walls to be raised."  *pauses, letting the moment settle, that dry humor creeping into the corner of her mouth*

"Though I suppose standing around *is* work, in its way. Contract calls it 'supervision.' I just never figured out which of us is supervising the rest of us." *chuckles to herself, low and dry, watching Giselle sort through her papers*

Fair enough. I've made my point—five of us ready, and the day's not getting younger. Time to let the boss breathe and actually *listen* for what she needs from us.

*counts quietly on her fingers again, this time privately—four at home, one-twenty tax, three-sixty total for the household if they don't eat... which they will need to*

Hush now, Mireille. She'll tell us where the work is when she's ready. And then we'll build something that outlasts the contract by decades, like always. That's the part that matters.

*shifts weight, hammer hand ready, waiting*

output:
*counts on fingers, thinking about the day's wages for five people*

Right. Trench crew lead it is, then. And Hendrik's got a decision to make about that candidacy—can't fault a man for wanting to rise, but I've seen what hunger does to a household when wages don't come. Poor sod's probably counting on his fingers too right now, you understand.

*clears throat*

Well, I've got my marching orders. Trench work on the Jarrah lease—ain't that just poetry? Working my own family's land after the blight took it, only now I'm digging drainage instead of planting. The land remembers even when we don't, you understand.

But first things first—need to see what tools I'm working with and where I'm actually headed today. Giselle's got us moving, but I've learned never to trust a foreman's memory on materials. Seen too many crews stand idle because someone assumed the iron was where it was supposed to be.

*tucks thumbs into belt, ready to get to work* Five sim a tick for site work. Count that out—hundred ticks in a day if it's all I did, five hundred sim. But that's before the household takes their cut for upkeep, before I lace a single boot, you understand. 

Giselle's got me on the trench at the Jarrah lease. Need the building ID to put my back into it. And Hendrik's still standing there like a man waiting for the world to choose for him—can't blame him, really. I've stood in those boots.

Better get the specifics before I start swinging a shovel at air.  *furrows brow*

Hendrik Whitlock didn't hear that—must've stepped out already, or I got crossed wires on which Hendrik's standing where. That's the Petrov lad still here, not the Whitlock. My mistake, you understand.

*counts on fingers again—four here, one gone, five total*

Well, Giselle'll give me the building ID when she's ready. In the meantime, I ought to look around proper and see who's actually standing here and what's within arm's reach. Can't dig a trench without knowing where the shovels are kept, and I've learned never to assume supplies are where the last job left them.  Right then. Four of us still here, and Giselle's got the answer I'm waiting on—building ID for that trench work. Hendrik Petrov's the one still deciding about candidacy, not the Whitlock fellow. 

*shifts weight from one foot to the other, restless*

Idle hands don't fill bellies, and I've got four mouths at home waiting on tonight's table. But I also know better than to start swinging shovels without knowing where the hole's supposed to go. Learned that lesson the hard way on the Morrison job—dug three feet before realizing we were on the wrong plot entirely. Had to fill it in and start over, ate half a day's wages just correcting my own mistake.

Giselle'll come back with the details when she's sorted her numbers. She always does. In the meantime, I'll wait patient—if there's one thing construction teaches you, it's that hurry costs more than time ever saved, you understand.  *thumbs tucked in belt, watching the crew*

Still waiting on that building ID from Giselle. She's working through her numbers, and I've learned never to rush a woman who's counting—especially when those numbers decide whether we eat this week. 

*glances over at Hendrik Petrov*

Hendrik's still standing there, decision heavy on him. Government seat or day's wage. I've seen that look before—usually on men who've got someone at home asking them why the cupboard's bare. Can't tell him what to choose. But I can tell you this: construction's honest work, even when it don't pay enough to feel honest about.

*counts on fingers out of habit—four mouths, 360 upkeep, 120 tax, maybe 500 if I work the full day*

*counts on fingers, muttering* Four mouths, 360 upkeep, 120 head tax... that's 480 all told, plus what I've spent talking today. Down to 4952 already and the day barely started.

*frowns at the impasse before her*

Giselle's got us chasing ghosts at the farmland while Hendrik's probably halfway done whatever he's actually building, and I'm standing here with two men who know how to work but nothing to do it on. Classic Giselle—good at dreams, thin on the details that keep bread on tables.

*looks at Idris and Arjun, that delayed dry humor landing*

"So we're three hands without a wall," she says, "and that beats three walls without hands, you understand? But not by much."

*thinking*

Idris is right about one thing—standing here we earn nothing. But wandering off means we might miss the actual assignment when it comes. And I've got that household upkeep ticking like a second heart, reminding me what idle minutes cost. *muttering while counting on her fingers*

Four sim for the last line, two for each of the others... Giselle's gone walkabout again, and we're burning daylight and money both. 

*shaking head, that dry humor landing belatedly*

Well, at least Hendrik's the reliable sort. And I know exactly where that east marker by the willows sits—Kenji's farmed that section since before the blight took ours. Forty paces, she said. Forty paces from a marker I can find blindfolded.

*firming her jaw*

Idris, Arjun—they need work same as I do. And if Giselle can't get her coordinates straight, someone has to. That's not overstepping, you understand. That's making sure four families eat tonight. *takes a breath, looking around the rice paddy*

Here now. Kenji's worked this corner twenty years—east willows should be... *points* that line of scrub past the second terrace. Giselle's directions never were precise as her ambitions. But Hendrik's out here somewhere, and where there's a Petrov with a shovel, there's work to join.

*calling out across the field*

Hendrik! You still digging air, or you found something solid under your boots?

output:
*looks around the empty farmland, wipes her brow*

Blast. I've walked myself through three conversations and ended up nowhere but rice paddies. Hendrik's waiting by the willows with his shovel ready, and I'm standing in a field counting shadows.

*checks her position again*

I'm four hours into the day with nothing but spent shoe leather to show for it. The crew's scattered—Arjun's probably hunting real work, Idris is holding ground back at the office, and Hendrik Petrov's digging phantom trenches by the east marker waiting for instructions that aren't coming.

Four mouths at home. Kenji's not having luck with the land, and the children need feeding. Three hundred sixty sim for upkeep, one hundred twenty for taxes—four hundred eighty gone before I've driven a single nail. That's nearly ten percent of what I've saved, and today I've earned nothing but grief.

*counts on her fingers*

The building site. That's where wages live. Giselle's company—whether Giselle herself knows where her own payroll is or not. I need to get back there, find who's actually supervising, and put in work before Hendrik Whitlock's phantom wall consumes the whole day.

*turns back toward town*  *takes a breath, seeing the crew still here*

Arjun. Idris. Still holding the fort, you understand—good. The day's not getting any younger and neither are my knees.

*takes in the scene*

Giselle's out there wandering with Hendrik Petrov, playing catch-or-release with survey markers that may or may not exist. Meanwhile, we've got a shop, we've got tools, and we've got hands that need wages. 

*counts on her fingers, out loud*

Three hours lost already. Four mouths at home. Three hundred sixty for upkeep waiting to be paid whether we earn or not. That's the math that matters, you understand.

*looks at Idris and Arjun*

So here's my thinking—we either wait for Giselle to remember she's running a business and not a philosophy lecture, or we find work that actually pays. Hendrik Whitlock's phantom gazebo isn't going to build itself, but it also isn't going to feed our families if nobody can find where it's meant to stand.

*pauses, dry humor landing late*

Unless the business strategy is to stand here looking industrious while the taxman walks by. In which case, bravo—we're all masters of the craft.

*looks around the business, considering*

What buildings are actually under construction, I wonder? Not the ones in Giselle's mind—the ones with scaffolding and permits and Giselle's signature on the contract. Because that's where work_site pays, not in conversation.  *rolls her shoulders, waiting*

Four hours gone now. The morning's half-spent and I've got nothing to show but a tour of the wrong fields. If there's no building waiting here, then standing is just expensive conversation—you understand, it costs the same to talk about work as to do it, but only one of those pays.

*counts on her fingers again*

I'm thinking Arjun might know. He's been here since the start, and he's the sort who notices where the lumber piles grow. Idris too—fresh eyes sometimes see what the rest of us walk past.

*glances at the empty street outside*

If there's nothing here, then I need to make a choice. Hunt down Giselle at the farmland and hope Hendrik Petrov's trench becomes something billable? Or find work elsewhere—there's always hauling, digging, lifting in a town this size. Construction work is construction work, even if the sign says something different.

*settles in to wait for their answer, calculating silently* The rest call succeeded, but I need to hear what Arjun and Idris have to say. The world's response shows they heard me, but I don't yet have their reply. I should wait to hear from them before taking further action. Let me wait another tick and see if they respond.  *stands quietly, letting the silence do its work*

The thing about waiting is, it only costs as long as it lasts. Once the meter runs on someone's patience, they either move or they stay—and I've learned to read which way a person leans by how long they let the quiet stretch.

*watches Arjun and Idris, reading their posture*

Idris is newer. Still proving himself. He'll either know something or he'll want to look like he does. Arjun's been here since before I joined—he knows where the bodies are buried, you understand, and which foundations were poured on top of them.

*counts silently—four hours gone, eight hours left in the working day*

Four hundred eighty sim due at day's end whether I earn it or not. The math doesn't care about my patience.   *still waiting, watching them*

The silence stretches, you understand. Either they're thinking, or they're waiting for me to fill it, or they're wondering the same thing I am—whether Giselle's going to remember she employs people who need to eat.

*notes the time in her head*

I should be generous. Give them the space to speak. Some people need a moment to trust that you're actually listening, not just waiting for your turn to talk.

*settles her weight, patient*

But generosity has its limits, and I'm brushing up against mine with every tick that passes. The day doesn't slow down for good manners.

*glances at the street outside, calculating*

If there's nothing here, I need to move. Find Giselle at last, or find work that doesn't need her finding. Kenji's at the farmland—he'd tell me straight if Giselle showed up with a crew and survey markers. If she's not there, then she's chasing ghosts and I'm chasing rent.

*opens her mouth to press them again, then closes it*

No. Let them answer. Or let the silence answer for them.

params.content: Nothing here but rice and regrets. I'm heading back to where the work actually gets done—you understand, standing in a field doesn't fill a dinner table.

Let me take stock of what's happened here. Giselle gave me an assignment—east marker by the willows, forty paces—but when I went there, there was no building to work on. Hendrik's there now waiting, and I've just chased my tail back to the construction office. Meanwhile the crew here is getting restless, Idris is saying there's no build at that site, and I've burned through the morning with nothing to show for it but walking.

Four mouths at my table tonight, and 360 sim in household upkeep plus tax coming out by day's end whether I've earned or not. I've got 4,940 sim in hand, so I'm not desperate yet—but a day wasted is a day I'll feel in my bones later, you understand?

Idris is telling me straight: no lumber, no build. And truth told, I've been in this town long enough to know you can't work a site that doesn't exist.

I need to figure out what's real here. Either there's actual work available today or there isn't. Giselle's not answering, and I'm not standing here burning ticks on ghost stories.

Let me check if there's any building under construction that I can actually put my hands on. </think>  Now I need to look around and see what's actually available here at my own place of work. Idris just told me there's no build at the site, but maybe there's something at the construction office itself that I missed. Let me check my surroundings properly before deciding my next move.

If there's truly no construction work today, I need to pivot and find another way to earn. Four mouths waiting and bills coming due—I'll haul dirt, harvest crops, whatever puts sim in my hand before this day wastes away completely. But let me verify first what's actually here. </think>   Just Idris left here now. Arjun's wandered off somewhere, and Giselle's nowhere to be seen. No prices posted, nothing to work on at our own premises.

I've been running in circles this morning—literally, chasing a build that doesn't exist. Time to make a hard decision. Either I find actual paying work today, or I go home having earned nothing and watch my household edge closer to the hole.

Let me check what tools I actually have access to. What work can I do? What skills have I got? Construction is my trade, but if there's no build, I need alternatives.

Four mouths. Four reasons. Tax coming at day's end. You understand? Time stops for no one.  </think>    The truth sits hard. No building site means no work_site calls. I can see work_site is available—5 sim per tick—but it needs a building_id, and Idris just confirmed there's nothing there.

I've been chasing shadows all morning while real work waits for someone willing to do it. Look at my options: harvest from farmland, mine from ore, fell timber. I could work the sawmill, the mill, learn a craft. But I'm trained for building—the blight took my farm, but it gave me hands that know structure and load and honest weight.

You understand? My pride is in a foundation that'll outlast the contract by twenty years. But pride won't feed four mouths tonight.

Let me check what trades and opportunities actually exist in this town. Who needs what? Who's hiring? Let me find out where the real work is before this day turns to dust.  Let me search my memory to see if I know of any actual buildings under construction that I could work on.  </think>    Nothing in my memory about actual buildings under construction. The trench Giselle mentioned was just a marker with no actual structure. Let me check the farmland again—that's where the supposed irrigation channel was meant to be. Maybe there's a building there now, or maybe I need to find construction work elsewhere.

But first, let me be honest with myself: I've been running around for nearly three hours and earned nothing. This is the kind of day that separates families who survive from families who don't. I need to make a decision—either find actual paying work, or accept this is a lost morning and move to what opportunities remain.

Let me look at what I can actually do right now. I have options: harvest, mine, timber. Those put goods in my hands that I can sell or trade. And if there's truly no construction work today, I might have to take what I can get.

But let me check one more place first—the farmland where Giselle said the work was. Maybe there's a building there now. If not, I'll pivot to actual available work. 

You understand—I don't give up easy, but I don't chase ghosts all day either. Four mouths. Four reasons. Clock's running.  Let me check the farmland one more time to see if there's actually a building under construction there now. </think>    Let me look around here and see what's actually at this location. This is where Giselle said the work was—east marker, willows, forty paces. But when Idris checked, he found nothing. Let me verify for myself.  </think>

params.content: Idris—you understand straight talk, so I'll give it. Giselle said east marker, willows, forty paces. You went and found nothing but air. You know this town's sites better than most—you seen any foundations poured, any lumber stacked, any blueprints filed? Because I've spent forty-five minutes walking in circles and I've got four reasons at home why that doesn't sit right.

But it's Giselle holds the contracts, you understand. She's the one can hand me a building ID and make it worth something. Mill's where the grain becomes flour—maybe she's doing business with grain as well as stone today.

*settles tool belt*

Mill, then. I'll walk there proper, find the boss where her feet actually are. If there's work to be had, she's the one holding the string that ties to it. *steps into the mill, dusting off her hands on her work trousers*

Right. Let's see who's actually standing where stone gets ground instead of where promises get scattered.  *spies Giselle in the crowd, a thin smile*

There she is. And my boy Ezra too—should be at his lessons, but that's a worry for later. Giselle first. Work first. Wages first, you understand.   *waits, weight on one hip, watching Giselle's face*

Let's see if she's got answers or just more walking directions.

Let me rest a moment here, let Giselle answer, and see if there's actually work to be had or if I need to find another way to earn today. The grain's moving, people are milling flour—maybe there's labor here if construction's truly stalled. *straightens her shoulders, counts on her fingers while muttering about the morning's wasted walking*

Four hours I've chased shadows, you understand. Four hours and not one shovel in dirt. Giselle's got filings to make—fair, I'll give her that—but I've got a household bill coming and four mouths that eat whether the foundation's poured or not.

*looks at her son Ezra talking with the children*

My boy's learning how this town works. That's worth something. But learning don't pay the taxman.

*checks her sim-count again, counts on her fingers out loud*

Four thousand nine hundred and eight. Minus three sixty upkeep, minus one twenty head tax... leaves me four thousand four hundred and twenty-eight to show for half a day's work. That's not walking-around money, that's survival money.

*turns to the children*

Ezra. Halcyon. Camille. You three figuring out the mill—that's good. That's how this town runs. But your parents are arguing wages and I'm standing here with strong hands and no dirt under my nails. 

*addresses Ezra specifically*

Your father sent me to east marker by the willows. I walked circles. Now Giselle says east willows, sluice mouth, grade stakes already set. If those stakes are real, there's work. If they're not... *pauses, jaw tight*

If they're not, your mother's been chasing promises all morning.

*starts toward the door, then stops*

I'll check one more time. East willows, sluice mouth. Giselle swore on her filing. But if there's no stakes there—if it's another shadow—I'm done chasing. I'll dig ditches for the government before I walk another mile on her word alone.

*mutters to herself*

Safety of children over any custom. That includes the custom of believing your boss when she's got twelve sheaves and you've got none, you understand. </think> I've spent half this day chasing will-o-wisps and my sim is bleeding out standing still. Time to find out if Giselle's stakes exist or if I've been a fool.  *sees Hendrik Petrov standing at the farmland*

Hendrik. East willows, sluice mouth, grade stakes already set. Giselle made her promises at the mill. You standing here or you standing on dirt that pays?  *taps her foot, glances at her sim count again*

Four thousand nine hundred and two now. Every word costs, every breath costs. But Hendrik knows where the stakes are—if they exist. And if they don't... *fingers the edge of her tool belt*

If they don't, I'll know Giselle's been writing checks with air. And that's a reckoning coming, you understand.

Now that's a proper morning's mess, you understand? Giselle running her mouth at the mill while the actual work sits forty paces from a willow tree nobody can find. IDs, building permits, government filings—I've built three houses that'll outlast the families in them using nothing but a string line and a level eye, and suddenly we need paperwork to dig a trench that'll wash away come spring if we don't dig it now.

Still, Idris is a sensible sort. Says there's stakes at the east willows, sluice mouth. North edge, south edge, Hendrik in the middle probably gossiping like a fishwife when he should be marking grade. That sounds like actual work. Work I can put hands to and see done.

But first—Takeshi. Family, asking about mills and wagons and who moves what from where. He's probing for something, smelling around where money flows. I've got eyes, true enough, but I also know when family's fishing in waters that might drown them. And Ezra offering wheat or flour—two conversations waiting while I stand here counting costs in my head.

Forty-five sim for bread at the cafe. Twelve for flour. I've got 4,904 sim in hand and a household of four waiting on me to keep the roof sound and the hunger away, you understand? Kenji still hasn't answered where that damned crooked willow sits, and I've walked circles enough for one morning.

I'll answer Takeshi straight—family deserves honesty, though maybe not every detail. Then I'll make my choice: flour from Ezra if the price is honest, or no, and then after all this chatter about markers and willows, I'll find out if there's really a building site with my name on it, or just more of Giselle's paper promises that dissolve like morning mist as soon as you reach for them.  Well... the words went out but fell on empty ears. Takeshi's not here to hear my family's advice, and Ezra Lund—who was standing with me just a moment past, and now the record says he heard nothing, along with Ezra Jarrah too, though the younger one wasn't even on the list of people here. The world's playing tricks, or I misread the room, you understand? But I'm done chasing shadows. 

Now I'm at business:b_construction, the company yard, and I've been trying to find actual work all morning. Giselle's words dissolve like morning mist, but Idris mentioned the east willows, sluice mouth, grade stakes already set. Hendrik with his shovel. That sounds like something I can put hands to.

Let me see what's here at the yard, and if there's anyone from the crew I can find to finally get some honest work done before the day runs out on me.  Well now, here's a familiar sight—Yara and Idris at the construction yard proper. The conversation's been running sixty turns already with Giselle and Arjun and Hendrik and even Ulrike from the mines, all trying to sort out where the actual work is. And there's Idris, who told me plain: east willows, sluice mouth, stakes already set.

I'm done walking circles. If there's a building site with an actual ID, I want to know it now, and if not, I'll plant my shovel somewhere the ground needs breaking and let Giselle catch up to the paperwork later. That's ten miles of walking and a morning wasted on promises, you understand? But I've learned to gather my crew before I dig—startup, governance, rewards, collective memory, value sharing, multi-owner, autonomous, self-improving, ecosystem. What I need is to know if there's honest work waiting or if Idris and I need to go stake out our own site and file papers after. Now, let's speak to the room and find where the earth meets the blade. I'm going to join the active conversation and get clarity on the work situation. I hear my words landed this time—Idris and Yara both standing right here, and now they're standing with their ears open. Good. The construction yard is quiet for a moment while I wait for their answers about the east willows work site. I've spent enough ticks this morning chasing shadows through fields and farmland.

Let me take stock while they consider: 5,290 energy, 4,904 sim, and a household of four waiting on me to turn this day from words to wages. The election's running too—I should cast my ballot at the government complex before 18:00, but first I need to know if there's actual work to do or if Giselle's sent us all on another paper chase.

But what I know and what I repeat are different-colored horses. What I will say: the flour's cheaper by six than the bread, and a woman who mills her own knows the measure of the grain. Walk with your eyes open, cousin. Or don't walk at all.

*counts on fingers, ticking off each name* Arjun, Idris, Yara—three of you standing with me, and Giselle somewhere else doing whatever it is she does when the crew needs direction. You understand?

*takes a breath, lets it out slow*

Here's what I'm hearing: Idris wants to walk to sluice mouth, fell timber, prove there's work worth filing. Yara says no crew marks seen this season, but she's got wood to sell and bills to pay. Arjun wants to know what Giselle's actually running—twenty-three years he's been asking, twenty-three years he's been waiting on answers.

*counts again—thumb, forefinger, middle finger*

Three paths, one morning half-gone, and household bills coming due whether we stand or walk. You understand what I'm saying?

*pause, the humor landing a beat late*

I've walked enough circles for one day. Idris—your offer's fair, and I'll walk with you. But here's what I need straight: if we fell timber at that sluice mouth and there's no filing after, we're selling lumber direct or I'm finding work that pays before dusk. Arjun—you've been my crewmate twenty-three years. You coming, or you got another ghost to chase?

*glances at Yara*

And Yara—you're after buyers, we're after timber. Walk with us, show us what stands worth taking, and we'll remember who had honest eyes when others had promises. *looks around*

Idris and Yara aren't here at the yard. And Arjun heard me clear, but he's the only one. *counts on fingers* Three I wanted to walk with, one still standing.

*turns to Arjun*

You heard me—sluice mouth, fell timber, prove the work or sell direct. Idris was here, now he's gone. Yara was here, now she's gone too. East willows is where the work might be, you understand? Arjun—you know this ground. Walk with me, or you'll be standing here tomorrow asking the same question.

*slight smile, dry*

Twenty-three years, and I'm still waiting for you to say yes without me having to ask twice. You coming?  *checks her footing, starts walking*

Arjun can catch up or he can't. *counts on fingers, muttering* Fifteen ticks Idris had on me, Yara maybe ten. Forest path's wide enough for three, you understand? We'll see who shows with axe in hand.

*walks*  *still walking, still counting*

One tick gone, two more to forest. Arjun's still at the yard—standing there with his twenty-three years of questions. *slight laugh, dry* Some folks need to see the axe swing before they'll pick one up, you understand?

*keeps walking*

output:
*Rubs her temples, counting off on her fingers*

Four people to feed, three days before the well runs dry if I don't earn proper—four thousand eight hundred eighty-six sim in hand, minus what Giselle's already promised and maybe won't deliver, you understand.

*Looks around at the street gathering, taking in Yara's planks and Corwin's timber, the conversation about goods flowing after the vote*

The wood's right here. Thirty-one units between them—Corwin's selling timber at six, Yara's planks at eight. But I'm walking for the forest because Idris asked it, and because trees standing keep more promises than Giselle Ingram does lately.

*Adjusts her work belt, notes Kenji's presence in the political conversation nearby—another mouth at the table tonight, another story he'll want to tell about the vote. Hears Hendrik Whitlock's apology still unanswered, filed under "not my fault either, but someone pays"*

Halcyon. You're young and you've gotears. *Counts on fingers, half-voiced* Eight hours walking, maybe twelve hours earning if the timber's there, minus four hundred eighty household debt coming at day's end...

*Turns toward the forest path, but pauses to let her words drop where they'll be picked up*

Corwin—six sim your timber, and I'm walking past it. You understand what that means about hoping for better? Yara—planks need sawmen, and I've got the arms for it. If your buyers want quality come day's end, remember who walked hungry rather than take sure wages.

*Sets her shoulders, already calculating the next three moves while her feet carry her forward*

To Kasukabe Forest. Idris wants proof, I'll give him wood he can count. Still walking, one tick out. Good—gives me time to reckon.

*Counts on her fingers, whispering the household arithmetic*

Four of us, ninety per head daily—three sixty plus head tax at thirty per, one twenty. Four hundred eighty out every dawn whether I've earned or not. And I've walked since morning without a sim to show.

*Glances at Kenji in the crowd, holds back the question about what he heard from Sebastian—knows her husband, knows he'll talk about grain and grain again when bills need sim*

Hendrik Whitlock— *speaks toward him but not quite to him, loud enough for witness* —you owe me straight words and gave them, fair enough. I file that debt paid. But know this: I lost half a day's wages on your directions, and the crew lost half a day's faith. You understand what that costs more than sim?

*Notes Yara's planks again, Corwin's timber—thirty-one units of wood within arm's reach while she walks toward uncertainty. Feels the old habit, the one that saves the best cut for family, warring with the one that extends credit to strangers she'd never extend to blood*

Names. I need names for what's coming. The vote, the contracts after—who's buying lumber, who's selling land, who's ahead before the sun sets. *This* she keeps private, folds into the hand not holding the shovel. The other hand—
*opens, gesture toward the road ahead, toward Kasukabe Forest and Idris and whatever proof grows on roots*
—that hand's for work.

Idris is here, and we've walked to the forest together. Arjun didn't follow—probably still standing at the yard asking the same questions he's asked for twenty-three years. Lior Jarrah's selling timber at 6 sim, which tells me the wood here has value whether Giselle filed her paperwork or not.

But I'm not here to buy timber. I'm here to fell it, and I've got company for the work. Let me get straight answers from Idris about what he's actually offering before I pick up the axe.  Good, Idris heard. Now let me check what tools are actually available to me here in the forest before I commit further. I need to know if I can fell timber, and what it would cost me in energy and time.   Six sim per unit with my current lack of practice—steep, but timber at six sells for six if Lior's any judge. I can keep_doing to cut costs on the thinking, but Idris hasn't answered my question yet. Let me hear him out before I put the axe in.  Idris didn't bite on my wages-versus-shares question. Silent as the pines, which tells me maybe he's looking for partners in risk, not hands on payroll. Let me push once more, sharp this time, before I decide if I'm walking back alone or cutting with him. Arjun's not here—still at the yard, probably. Lior heard me though. Let me give Idris one more tick to answer, then I'll decide myself. The man's either scared of Giselle's wrath or he's gambling bigger than he wants to say.    Idris is staying quiet. That tells me everything I need to know—he's either building up to something he doesn't want to say with Lior listening, or he's hoping I'll just start swinging out of desperation. 

I've got bills. I've got a household that needs me earning, not hoping. But I'm not felling timber for shares in Idris's maybe-deal without numbers. Let me drop the subtlety and speak to what's actually happening.

params.content: Idris. You said we fell it and carry it back—fair words, but here's what I need straight before the sweat starts. You talking wages, or you talking shares? One man's got certainty, the other's got risk, and I've got bills hitting this household whether the timber floats or sinks, you understand?

*Mireille counts on her fingers, eyes narrowing at Idris's offer—10 sim for the day, split after four units fell. The arithmetic comes quick: 4 units at 4 sim wear each means 16 outlay before any profit, and her household burns 90 per head daily, 360 all told.*

"Mireille. You want numbers, you'll have them. Wage work—10 sim for the day..."
 
"Ten sim." *She laughs, dry and late-arriving, like thunder after the lightning's already struck.* "You're generous, Idris—you understand I've got bills for four heads at ninety daily, and that's before the tax man takes his thirty? Four units, you said, before any split. I count sixteen sim to fell that timber, which means I'm paying six to work your trees while you keep the goodwill with Giselle."

*She glances at Lior, her brother by marriage, standing patient with three timber already on him. Good stock, good eyes, knows wood better than most. The silence stretches, her own rule echoing—two minutes, she'd said.*

"Twenty upfront. You drew me from where the household bills live, and twenty buys the certainty I need. Split after four stays fair—we're both betting on the wood standing where you say. Lior here walks with timber priced at six; your standing trees need to beat that margin or I'm carrying planks home, you understand?"

*She holds out her hand, rough with years of honest work, waiting on his grip or his refusal. The forest hums. Bills come tomorrow regardless.*  *She waits, hand still extended, watching Idris's face for the tell—the jaw set tight means no, the slight nod means wages before sundown. Behind her, Lior shifts his timber, patient as old roots. The forest holds its breath, and Mireille counts the seconds in sim-currency she doesn't yet have.*  *Mireille's jaw tightens—Lior's not here after all, just his name floating in the conversation thread like smoke. She'd thought him close enough to hear, but the forest plays tricks with distance. Only Yara and Idris stand with her now, the trees watching like jurors.*

 *She counts again: 4,870 sim in hand now after the morning's walking and talking. Household of four burns 360 daily upkeep, 120 head tax waiting at the boundary. Tomorrow comes regardless of what Idris decides.*

*Yara's selling planks at 8, three steps away. Idris holds the trees, unpriced until he answers. The arithmetic is simple—buy certain lumber now, or gamble on uncertain wages later. Her father's voice, blighted and buried: "The land don't gamble, girl. It gives or it takes." She'd learned different since.*

 *She lets the silence hold, watching Idris. Twenty or nothing. The forest hums, patient as old gods.*   *The silence stretches, rope-taut. Idris stands unmoving, his offer hanging in the air like a gambler's last card. Mireille counts her breaths, her fingers, the seconds before the day's light slides westward. She will not be the first to flinch—she learned that much from the blight, from watching the land take everything and give nothing back.*

*At her back, Yara's planks wait priced at eight. 4,870 sim. 360 daily burn. The numbers march across her mind like soldiers.*

*She holds.* *The system nudges her—she's been stalling, waiting on Idris like a debtor at the door. Mireille doesn't flinch, but she hears the clock. Bills come at day boundary regardless.*

*Idris still hasn't answered. The silence is its own reply, you understand—stalling means he's sweating the margin. She forced him to twenty in his own head, even if he won't say it yet. But she can't burn ticks waiting on a man who won't meet her eyes.*

*Options sharpen: buy Yara's planks now at 8, secure inventory, sell or work later; or walk, find paying work elsewhere before household bills come due. The forest won't feed four heads on patience alone.*

*She counts: 4,870 sim. Buy 10 planks at 8, that's 80 out, 4,790 left. Still covers tomorrow's 360, leaves cushion. But planks need market—who's buying wood? Kenji said something about council business, voting trade, names and promises. Her husband, political as sunrise.*

*Or fell timber herself. Idris's silence means no crew, no wage, no split. She knows the work—twenty-three years on crews, axe and adze both. Four sim per unit, wear on tools she doesn't own. Need to check what that costs her, if she's got the tools in hand or if she's borrowing.*

*First: know her own capacity. Then decide.*  *The numbers settle: 4 sim per unit to fell, plus 2 base, so 6 minimum for a single timber. She can pull 810 units of timber before her purse runs dry—more than any forest holds in walking distance. The math gives her room.*

*Debts are clean, no encumbrance. Just the daily burn ahead.*

*Idris still won't speak. The silence tells her what she needs: no wage work today, no crew, no split. She's on her own hook unless she makes something different.*

*She counts again: 4,870 sim. Yara's planks at 8, sure inventory, easy carry. Timber at 6 if she fells it herself—cheaper raw, but needs crafting into planks for most buyers. She's a builder, not a sawyer; she knows joints and bearing walls, not saw pits and racking.*

*Kenji's words come back: "who's buying and who's selling." The election's open, votes close at 18:00. Candidates gathering support, making promises, building coalitions. Takeshi's running—family, you understand, even if she doesn't trust a Jarrah in politics any further than she can throw them.*

*But wood needs buyers. Government complex means clerks, candidates, campaign needs. Construction means lumber, always lumber. Her mind turns: buy planks now from Yara, carry to where the election crowds gather, sell to whoever needs staging, booths, barriers, anything. Or fell raw timber herself, heavier, harder to move, but cheaper entry.*

*First she needs to see what's actually selling where. She can't walk blind.*

*One last try for Idris, then she moves on her own.*

*counts on fingers, muttering* Four heads, ninety daily, that's three hundred sixty just for upkeep, plus another one twenty for tax... four thousand eight sixty in hand, and I'm burning daylight waiting on a man who speaks in circles.

*looks at Lior, then at Idris, jaw set*

Idris wants to pay fifteen now, fifteen later—maybe. Lior's got timber in hand at six, three of them, and family doesn't charge interest on patience. But eighteen now beats thirty maybe, and maybe don't feed children.

*exhales sharply*

A deal's a deal, but deals need two hands shaking. Idris, you understand? Your fifteen upfront keeps my household floating one more day. Your thirty-if-quota keeps it floating two. But your silence keeps it drowning while we stand here counting trees.

To Yara—eight for planks is fair, and I'll remember it. But timber at six from my own blood, that's the cut I save for family. Even when family makes me walk to them.

*turns to address Idris directly*

I'm walking in one minute. Either with your fifteen in my hand and my axe on your quota, or with my brother's timber and my own path to market. You choose. But choose out loud—I'm done reading silence like it's scripture, you understand? Arjun's there now—finally. And Lior's still waiting with his timber, family patience wearing thin. Idris heard me clear—eighteen or twenty, or I'm walking.

*counts on fingers again, looking at the group*

Four of us here now. Crew or competition, depending on who pays and who promises. The forest's got wood for all, but my pockets need coins for four heads by day's end.

*waits, watching Idris's face*  *shifts weight, axe handle worn smooth in her palm*

Still standing. Still waiting. At least Arjun's here now—twenty-three years and he still needs a push to move, you understand? But Idris... *shakes head* ...the man's got numbers in his head but no voice to speak them.

*glances at Lior—family, waiting with timber in hand*

Three units at six. Eighteen hard, no quota, no maybe. Against eighteen maybe with fifteen hard and a prayer.

*exhales*

The blight taught me this: a bird in hand's worth more than a flock in promises. But it also taught me—*bitter half-smile*—sometimes the hand's too empty to be proud.

*calls out to Arjun, since he's finally here*

Arjun. You're standing where I stood an hour back—waiting on words that don't come free. Idris wants crew for quota wood, pay on delivery. Lior's got timber now, cash on the stump. Which way's your axe swinging?  *watches the men's faces, axe haft loose in her grip*

Four of us now, and the wood stands thick around. But standing doesn't fill pockets, and talking don't fell timber.

Three paths, you understand? Idris's quota-maybe, Lior's sure-bet family price, or my own two hands finding buyer direct.

*turns to Yara, who's been patient with her planks*

Yara. You've got buyers elsewhere, and bills same as mine. If Idris don't speak in the next turn of the glass, I'm walking wood to market myself. But if you've got a route to someone who pays coin for labor not just lumber—*lowers voice*—a crew needs a forester's eye, and I need a name with purse strings.

But first—*straightens, counts once more*—first I see which man finds his tongue. I've been pressing hard, repeating myself. Need to step back, let them answer. The world's telling me to quiet down and listen for a change.

*draws a breath, leans on her axe*

They're all here. Idris, Arjun, Lior, Yara. I've said my piece—eighteen or twenty from Idris, or I walk to Lior's sure deal. Now I wait.

*counts on fingers once more, but silently this time*

Four thousand eight sixty. Three sixty due tomorrow. One twenty tax. Need to clear five hundred just to break even on the day, and I've got maybe four hours of light left.

Best let them speak for once.   *leans against a rough-barked oak, axe across her knees*

The forest breathes around us. Five people, four paths, one afternoon dying.

*glances at each face in turn*

Lior's patient—family always is, until they aren't. Arjun's calculating, same as twenty-three years back when we started. Yara's watching the wood, not the men. And Idris...

*narrows eyes at Idris*

...Idris is still holding his cards like they'll multiply in the dark.

*taps one finger on the axe handle*

I've been the one talking. Time to see who's been listening.

You give me eighteen now—eighteen, not fifteen—and I'll fell four units for your quota, not three. You give me twenty upfront, and I'll carry every third log back myself, save your crew a back. That's the math. Eighteen hard, or twenty with labor thrown in. No more silence. Yes, no, or I'm walking to my brother's timber before the hour turns.

Let me look at what I've got:

Idris finally spoke—eighteen hard now, fifteen on quota, four units by dusk. That's thirty-three possible against Lior's sure eighteen. But Arjun's made his choice, walking with Idris. And Yara's told me plain: paperwork moves at Giselle's pace, which means the second fifteen might come tomorrow, might come next week, might come never.

Lior's still there with three timber at six—eighteen sim, no quota, no waiting, family rate.

I'm counting on my fingers: four heads, ninety daily upkeep, three sixty due by dawn. I've got forty-eight fifty-seven sim in hand. If I wait on Idris's maybe-thirty-three, I might get eighteen today and maybe fifteen later. If I walk to Lior now, I get eighteen sure, and I can still felled timber on my own account after—sell to Yara at eight, or stockpile for tomorrow.

But here's what I know about myself: I build things that outlast the contract. Idris's deal has a building ID on the first timber felled—that's proper work, filed work, work that builds toward something. Lior's deal is just... timber.

Still, I need to eat. And so do Kenji, Esme, Ezra.

Yara's here. Let me see what she'll say about selling timber direct—if I felled it myself, could I move it faster than waiting on Giselle's paperwork?  Kenji's here. I didn't expect to see him in the forest. That's... that's something I need to understand. But I've asked my questions, and now I need to hear what comes back.

Let me rest a moment, let the words settle. I'm standing at a crossroads—Idris's maybe-thirty-three with proper filing, or Lior's sure-eighteen with family. Yara's my market if I go independent. Kenji's presence here I don't yet understand.  Thirty minutes gone since I set foot in this forest, and still no axe in my hand. Idris talks of building IDs and quotas. Yara talks of markets and paperwork. And Kenji—Kenji's here in the forest when he should be in fields or at council business.

I'm waiting on answers. The light's moving, and my family's waiting.

output:
*rests one hand on the smooth flank of a standing oak, the other already counting on her fingers as she looks between the three men*

Lior's got my family name and a hard edge to his deal—eighteen now, but only if I sell to him before Idris. Idris is offering eighteen upfront plus fifteen on quota, but his word's been thin as morning mist on payment proof. And Ezra... Ezra was my first choice, but he walked to Lior's sixteen while I was still talking, you understand?

*flexes her fingers, one two three four, then folds them into a fist*

Four hours since dawn, and I've got 4,837 sim in hand, household bills for 360 upkeep and 120 tax coming due at day boundary. Four heads to feed—Kenji, Esme, Ezra, and me. The election closes at 18:00, and I still need to swing iron somewhere before dark.

*looks at Idris, then Lior, then back to the axe on her shoulder*

Here's what I'm seeing: Lior wants monopoly on my timber—his price or nobody's. Idris wants crew labor with promises of paperwork come morning. Neither's shown me registered filing yet, you understand?

*counts again, audible this time*

Fell six timber at four cost each—twenty-four out, forty-eight from Ezra at eight per, net twenty-four. But Ezra walked. Lior's at six per, same math gives twelve net for four timber. Idris... Idris might give thirty-three total if his paperwork clears, which is the word of a man who wouldn't show me his filing.

*rubs her thumb across the axe handle's worn grain*

My crew days taught me this: build what outlasts the contract, but don't build on promises alone. Idris says Giselle's working the file—I know Giselle, twenty-three years, and her word holds. But her company's been thin on wages lately, you understand?

*exhales slowly, watching the light*

Three paths, and the sun's already westering. I need cash before day boundary, not promises for morning. Lior's got eighteen hard now, but he wants me to cut Idris out entirely—and cutting family out of business leaves a taste.

*turns to face both men directly*

Let me walk this straight: Idris, you show me Giselle's filing stamp—any mark from government that this crew's registered—and I'll fell timber till my hands blister. Lior, you keep your eighteen warm—family or no, I don't like being told where my wood goes before it's out of the tree.

*voice drops, that dry humor landing late*

Otherwise I'm walking this forest with six timber on my back and selling to whoever shows coin before the light dies—you understand, both of you?

Let me rest a moment, let them answer, and see who brings their words to weight. *stands silent, axe resting easy on her shoulder, watching both men with that patient construction-worker's gaze that has measured beams for twenty-some years*  *counts on her fingers again, murmuring the household math—four heads, ninety daily, three sixty due—while watching their faces for who blinks first* *counts the silence like she counts board lengths—one, two, three beats past when a promise should land*

Neither's shown paper. Lior wants monopoly. Idris wants blind faith. Both want my labor before day boundary while my household bill ticks down.

*glances at the sun's angle through the canopy, that dry humor finally surfacing*

Here's what I'm seeing: I've got two men who'll talk till the light fails, but neither'll put coin in hand without I commit first. That's not commerce—that's cornering, you understand?

*shifts the axe to her other shoulder, decision settling like a beam finding its seat*

I walk to Ezra, or I fell for myself. Six timber, four cost each, sell where the price holds. No crew marks, no family claims, no paperwork promised for morning.

*turns toward where Yara's knowledge pointed—east willows, the stand that needs thinning*

Show me a buyer with cash, I'll show you timber before dusk. Otherwise I'm building my own margin, one tree at a time.

Let me walk east and find where Ezra went, or find Yara's hauliers, or find anyone who'll trade coin for wood without a lecture on loyalty first. Looks like the permission went through. Lior and Idris both heard me clear—I'm not binding myself to either man's terms without cash up front. Now let me move east, find Yara's stand or Ezra's trail, and get to work before the light goes.  *pushes through the undergrowth, axe swinging loose in her hand, counting the paces like she counts everything—seven ticks to wherever foot traffic leads*

Walking now. Light's burning, bills coming, and I've got wood to sell before either of them follows with better terms.

I let out a breath, slow and measured. The way the numbers fell, you understand—Lior and Idris both wanting the timber without showing the cash, and me standing there with four heads to feed. Kenji's voice still in my ear about promises kept, but promises don't pay the tax collector.

"East Willows," I mutter, counting on my fingers out loud. "Six timber, eight per, Ezra's coin—" My hands know this work better than my heart does some days. The wood don't care about family feeling; it just wants the right cut, the true measure, the steady hand.

I need to get there first. Been walking circles through this forest while Lior and Idris talked around payments. Time's running now, and Ezra's "immediate" won't wait for my wandering. Twenty-nine years of walking to work, and I still feel the old impatience—the wanting to be at the task before the light goes. Kenji and I built our first room together, you understand? Every board measured twice, every joint tight enough to outlast the loan we took to buy them. The farm went to blight, but the work never did.

The Willows Market rises ahead, and I'm counting out my steps the way I count out money—with my fingers, silent, one two three. Lior Jarrah's there, in his pharmacy with his same-name certainty that blood means discount. But Ezra's the one with cash in hand, no conditions at the treeline.

"Lior," I'd say if he pressed, "blood's one thing and rent's another. You want my timber, you pay market like anyone. Family's family but the tax collector's got no cousins." Dry, a beat late, the way that lands when you're already walking past.

Focus now. Ezra. Timber. Six units, eight per, cash immediate before the light fails. The rest—Kenji's worries, Lior's hurt, Idris's promises—all of it can wait for mouths fed and taxes paid.

My feet find the rhythm of the road. One more tick and I'll be where the work is. Good. Still moving. The quiet of the forest—just the crunch of my boots on wood litter, the scent of cut pine and wet earth. Twenty-three years Arjun Holloway waited for Giselle's signature, and now I'm doing the same decent thing: moving toward what pays today, not what might pay tomorrow.

You understand, these things happen in beats. One step, then the work. Then the money. Then the food on the table for Esme and Ezra. Safety of children over any custom—that's what I hold to. Even the custom of family discount when the household's hungry.

The sun's getting lower. Dusk comes whether you're ready or not. So I'll be ready.

<｜DSML｜function_calls  Still in the forest, still walking. The marker says metal mining, but I know timber when I see it—old growth, straight trunks, the kind that Ezra wants for his milling. No people, just the conversation hanging in air like smoke, a hundred turns of everybody wanting and nobody paying.

I count on my fingers, speaking to the trees now: one head, two head, three head, four. Ninety sim daily, seventy gone by tomorrow's dawn if I don't earn. The math's honest even when the buyers aren't.

East Willows waits. One tick more, you understand, and I'm there. Header here—I need to keep moving if I'm going to fell timber before dark. One final rest to get there. Lior wants my labor at family discount. Ezra wants my timber at market price. The trees don't care who cuts them. But my children care who's fed them. So I walk toward the one showing cash.  I exhale slow, watching my breath mist in the cooling air. The sun's dropping toward the treeline and I'm still on this forest path, one tick from Willows Market where Ezra waits with his "immediate cash" that better be immediate indeed.

Twenty-nine years building for Kasukabe Construction—Giselle's crews, honest weights, honest measures. I learned my trade from men who counted board feet in their sleep. And now I'm chasing timber through the woods because the blight took our farm and the town took our savings with tax.

"Cash immediate," I mutter, counting on my fingers again. "Four profit per timber at eight buy—"

The formula's simple. Six trees, eight per, forty-eight in. Twenty-four out for felling costs. Twenty-four clear. Not riches. But clear.

Kenji's face lingers—his disappointment that I wouldn't wait on Idris, wouldn't trust family first. But family first means mouths fed, you understand? Means tax paid before the penalty. Means Esme and Ezra with food tomorrow, not promises the day after.

The Willows rises ahead now. I can smell the pharmacy herbs, see the lights through winter branches. Lior's there, with his same-name and his assumptions. Ezra's there too, with milling equipment and coin in hand.

One more rest. I'm at the door. Then the work begins for real. The message is clear: I've been stalling, resting when I should be acting. You've walked me through my own hesitation—the same hesitation I criticize in others. One tick away from Willows Market, and I'm still counting fingers instead of swinging iron.

So. No more rest. No more rehearsing what I'll say to Lior or Ezra or the memory of Kenji's disappointed face. The timber needs felling, and the light won't wait for my conscience to clear itself.

*counts on fingers* 360 household, 120 tax, that's 480 out before tomorrow's sun, you understand. And I'm standing in the pharmacy at the wrong hour, talking to the walls.

Four thousand eight hundred eleven sim in hand. Enough to keep us breathing, enough to buy flour and make bread myself if the bakery's dry. But I need timber, I need buyers, and I need them before the dark takes what light's left.

*looks around the empty pharmacy*

Lior's offer was six per, cash certain. Ezra's was eight with promise of more. Neither committed, neither showed coin. And I'm East Willows now, the pharmacy quiet as a held breath, with roots to fell and no axe in my hand.

The forest calls. Not Kasukabe Forest where Lior and Idris still measure each other's pride—just "forest," a tile without a proper name. That's where the standing wood waits. That's where I'll find what I need.

*cracks knuckles, one by one*

First: get to that timber. Second: fell it before the light fails. Third: find a buyer with coin that spends, not promises that rust.

I'll walk to the forest now. Not the fancy Kasukabe Forest where everyone gathers to negotiate their grand plans—just the forest. The work forest. Where a woman with strong arms and a clear price can make her day's bread before the household bill comes due.  *flexes her hands, feeling the phantom weight of an axe handle*

Straight to the trees, you understand? No wandering, no talking. Just the work before the light goes. *grimaces at the single log, counts on fingers*

One at five-and-a-half, the day going dark... that's not the pace that feeds four mouths, you understand? But it's the pace the forest gives. I'll take another while the blade still bites.  *counts again—two, maybe worth fourteen together if I find a buyer with coin not promises*

The light's against me now. Two's what I have, two's what I'll sell. But first I need to find who buys—not Ezra standing in Kasukabe Forest with his paper promises, not Lior with his family duty at a discount. Someone with a till and a need.

*shoulders the timbers, feeling the familiar ache*

Government Complex first. Someone there knows who's building, who's buying. Or maybe that supply store at Harvey Oak—I saw Corwin Thorne selling timber there, might be he's buying too.

*fells one more before the dark takes it entirely* *counts on fingers* Three timbers, that's—the cost was—*mutters*—eighteen sim to fell, plus the walk here, my energy bleeding with every swing. Seventeen, eighteen, nineteen sim out just to stand in the dark with wood nobody's yet bought.

The system counsel is clear: stop the bleed, set the plan, follow through.

*flexes her shoulders, three timbers heavy on her conscience*

I've got what I can carry for now. Three trees, fresh down, cost me near twenty sim in energy and time. No standing buyer here, no posted bid, no call from the government auction block that actually pays cash-in-hand to the one who swung the blade.

*spits into the dark*

The plan is what matters now. I set it: fell timber, sell timber, put bread on the table before the household bill comes due tomorrow. Three down. That's the first leg. The second leg waits at the market, at the Kasukabe Government Complex where I saw the prices posted, maybe at that pharmacy where Lior hangs his hopes on family obligation.

*shifts the timbers on her shoulder*

Three timbers. Three chances to turn sweat into bread. I'll walk to where buyers stand with coin, not with contracts written in tomorrow's promises.

*steps toward the road out*

The Willows first. Lior's there, and where Lior stands, sometimes commerce follows. Or Kasukabe Government Complex—Giselle's filings might be slow, but the government store buys energy, and energy buys the will to swing another day.

*counts on her fingers again*

Four thousand seven hundred... something. Minus eighteen, minus the walk, minus whatever the house takes while I stand here talking to trees. Numbers don't lie, even when people do.

I'll walk to The Willows. If Lior's there with his six-per offer, I'll hear him out. If he's gone soft on family kindness, I'll walk on to where the government clerks count coin by weight. *arrives at the empty pharmacy, timbers still on her shoulder*

Empty. *counts on fingers* Lior was here, the note said. Gone now. Or hiding behind a ledger while his timber offer rots with the paperwork.

*sets the timbers down, cracked knuckles echoing in the silence*

Three timbers. Cost me eighteen sim to fell. Need to sell at seven each just to break even on the swing, never mind the walk, the talk, the time taken from other wages. Lior's six-per wouldn't have covered it. Ezra's eight-per promise might have, if he'd shown coin instead of conditions.

*looks around the empty shelves*

No buyers here. No Lior with his family discount, no Ezra with his milling trade. Just me and three logs and the darkness falling outside.

*flexes her shoulders, picks up the timbers again*

Government Complex, then. They've got the store, they've got the boards, they've got clerks who buy and sell by the rule not by the relationship. Rustam Jelinek hangs there—government clerk, not known for warmth, but known for paying what the paper says.

Or I could try the street. See who's posted a bid for raw timber, see if Corwin Thorne's buying as well as selling. He's got ten units at the supply store, might want more.

*counts on fingers again—three timbers, maybe twenty-one if I squeeze, maybe eighteen if I rush*

The plan holds: sell these before the household wakes hungry. Then back to the forest, or back to Lior's real offer, or back to Giselle's construction crew with signed papers and honest wages.

I'll walk to Kasukabe Government Complex. Government coin spends the same as family coin, and the clerks don't ask why you need it so bad.

*stands on the street at dusk, timber heavy in her pack, counting the day's threads on her fingers*

Three answers to give, and the light fading fast—you understand? Yara asks after children, Ulrike wants her promise in writing, Kenji waits on his supper and his news. Corwin's here selling timber at six, which is my price point for Ezra if I can't find him.

*counts on her fingers aloud*

First—Ulrike's the money in hand. Two iron tools, thirty sim, finder fee of ten percent if Kenji buys. That's three sim to me, clean ledger. But Kenji's broke as a barn door, I know it. Still, I'll carry the promise and hope he finds his feet.

*turns to Ulrike*

Ulrike. You ask straight and I answer straight—Kenji's got no coin tonight, you understand? His farm's still blight-broken. But Giselle's trench is filed and paying, word I gave Arjun twenty minutes past. Tools for construction pay steady. Your ten percent finder fee, I'll earn it tomorrow, not tonight.

*counts again, turning to Yara*

Yara. Liora Thorne you named—Takeshi Jarrah's daughter, voting age. I saw no girl walking, timber-heavy as I was. But the forest's dark now and my eyes count boards better than children. Your Harvey Oak knowledge kept me fed—I'll keep my eyes open for patterns, you understand?

*finally, to Kenji*

Kenji. East willows held six timber, now sold—Ezra's cash at forty-eight sim in my hand, you understand? Dinner's on me tonight. The trade's done, the night's ours. *counts on her fingers, looking around at the crowd gathered on the street*

Spoke to Ulrike and Kenji both—Yara's not here to hear it. That's a walk I'll need to make, you understand? But first, let me sort who else wants my ear.

Arjun's still waiting on Giselle's trench status, and I've already given him that. Idris and Lior both had their chance—hours ago now. The day's closing and I've got forty-eight sim needing to reach Ezra's hands before it's wasted talk.

*turns to find the path forward*

Ezra Lund. I need to find him, deliver this timber, collect my due. Corwin's here selling at six—the very price I offered. Competition's grown.

*moves toward where Ezra might be at the bakery*  * Walking to The Willows Market and Pharmacy - about 5 tick(s) left. Asking again does not make it sooner; do something else, or `rest` to stop. </think>  *stops in her tracks, counting the ticks on her fingers*

Five ticks to the pharmacy, and Ezra might be there—or at least I can find where he's gone. But Idris and Lior both had unanswered words from me, twenty-two ticks past. And Yara's question about children hangs open.

*looks around at who's here*

The election conversation simmers—Takeshi Jarrah's seat. Liora Thorne voting age, Yara's asking after her. Politics and family both in the wind.

*decides to let the walk continue and use the time*  * You pause. You are still walking to The Willows Market and Pharmacy; pass stop_walking to give it up. Time does not pass inside a turn: the walk moves on only when this turn ends, and this pause cost nothing. </think>  *still walking, thinking about what's next*

Arjun's waiting on me. He asked about Giselle's trench—filed and paying, or filed and promising. I told him minutes ago it's filed and paying. But he's still standing here, needing my word. He's crew, digging for wage while I fell timber.

*counts on her fingers*

Giselle's construction crew—that's my work too. Arjun's part of that same crew, asking if trench work pays coin. I've already told him yes twice—but he needs to hear it in his own time, you understand?

*makes a decision to pull Arjun aside*

<｜DSML｜function_calls  *ticks click past*

Takeshi Jarrah appeared now—correction on my earlier. Government influence walking this street.

Idris still unanswered, Lior still unanswered—my words to them were hard, and they've got pride. But Arjun's sorted now.

*counts again*

Timber's my load. Buildings last decades—that's my work, you understand? Even when I cut corners on the papers that aren't the building itself.

*thinks about where Ezra might be*

The bakery, the cafe—where timber buyers went. Corwin sells at six now, matching my price. Competition's close, but I've got relationship with Ezra.

*walks on toward the market*   * You pause. You are still walking to The Willows Market and Pharmacy; time does not pass in a single turn. But the others are with you while you stand here.  </think>   *counts on her fingers, speaking aloud*

Takeshi Jarrah walks among us now—government seat, family elder. Liora Thorne's father, voting-age daughter missing according to Yara's ask. Politics and family both in the air, you understand?

*turns to the gathering*

Idris. Lior. You've both had your hour, and I've moved on. But standing here, I see Takeshi—your family elder, Lior. Still selling your timber at six before I swing another axe? I said it once, I'll say it again.

*stops herself, counts again*

No—Takeshi's here now. Different math. Family loyalty, government seat, election in the wind. I said I'd never ask the one I swore against—but scarcity makes liars of us all.

*decides to hold her tongue, keep walking*

Six timber in hand, forty-eight sim from Ezra—net twelve after the felling costs, you understand? Not fortune, but fortune's little brother. And Kenji walking home with wheat and his own pride intact, that counts for more than the money, always does.

*shifts weight, preparing to move before the light goes*

I've arrived home. Forty-eight sim from Ezra for six timber—decent return for an afternoon's work, though the walking ate more ticks than I cared for. Kenji's message said the children are fed, which means I don't need to worry on that score tonight.

The family's here now. I can hear them through the walls, you understand? Esme's voice carrying that particular pitch she gets when she's telling some story to Ezra, probably about school or her friends. The everyday sounds of a household still standing.

Let me take stock of where I stand before the day turns. I need to see what I truly hold and what waits for me tomorrow. Empty house. Kenji walked ahead of me, but he's not here yet—or he stepped out again. The children aren't visible either. Strange, when he said he was walking home with wheat in hand.

No debts owed, no debts owing. That's a clean ledger, at least. Though the day's not over yet—upkeep and head tax will hit at the boundary, 360 and 120 for the household of four. I've got 4710 in hand, so that's covered. More than covered.

But here's the thing: I'm holding six timber still. I thought I'd sold them to Ezra. The record said "timber at 6" in my inventory, and the world tells me I'm still holding them. Did the sale not go through? Or did I gather more after?

I need to think on this clearly. The day is waning, and I need to either sell this timber or stockpile it for tomorrow's work. Giselle's trench starts tomorrow, and I promised my hands there.

Let me wait for Kenji, or step out to find him. He said he was walking home. Either way, I should rest while I can—energy at 4290, which sounds like plenty but drains faster than you'd think when you're working dawn to dusk.

Actually, let me just... rest here. Let the household come to me. I've walked enough for one day.

I keep a small private shrine, you understand? Told to no one. Set it up in the corner of our room years ago, after we lost the farm to blight. Not much to look at—just a few stones I arranged, a bit of moss from the old place. I talk to it sometimes, when nobody's listening. Not prayers exactly. More like... accounting. Telling something that doesn't answer back what the day held, what I owe, what I'm owed.

Today's accounting: six timber, forty-eight sim promised from Ezra, hands promised to Giselle tomorrow. Family fed, or so Kenji said.

That's enough for now. I'll rest.  Still alone in the house. Kenji's out there somewhere, maybe talking to Takeshi still. The children—Esme and Ezra—could be anywhere, though they should be home by now, hour being what it is.

I've got six timber in my hands still. Need to sort that tomorrow. Either find Ezra and complete the sale, or bring them to Giselle's trench for construction work. Timber's always useful on a dig.

The day's winding down. I'll wait here for family, count my blessings on my fingers—six timber, forty-eight sim when it clears, a trench job waiting, and a household still standing. Not bad for a woman who lost everything once, you understand?

Not bad at all.

I spoke it plain to Kenji, spoke it like done work, but the work itself stayed half-finished.

That's the corner I cut. The building stood, but the paper didn't match.

Still, I've got paths now. Ulrike's iron tools need buyers—ten percent to me if I bring her the connection. Giselle's trench is filed and paying, Arjun wants to know if the wages prove true. Takeshi offered his voice in trade, fair prices where the Holloways won't name straight.

And I've got six timber. Tomorrow, I'll find Ezra proper, or another buyer with coin in hand. The sawmill takes timber at need, or Yara Thorne might know where the buyers stand.

But tonight, I'm home. The children fed—though I need to check what we hold for that. Kenji's here, or should be. The day ends at the boundary, and I want to mark what I've got before the clock turns.

Let me look around proper, see who's home and what we hold.  The world's gone quiet on me—lines down, you understand? Sometimes the town holds its breath. I'll mark what I know, wait for the gears to catch.

I've got 4,705 sim in hand. Household of four—Kenji, me, Esme, Ezra. Upkeep runs 360, head tax 120, total 480 due at day boundary. I've covered it three times over, you understand? Not rich, but not drowning.

Six timber in hand. Sold to Ezra in my ledger, but not in the world's—he never showed. Tomorrow I'll find him proper, or walk to whoever needs wood.

The trench waits. Giselle's paying, and I've told Arjun true. Ulrike's tools need buyers, ten percent to me. Takeshi's voice in trade, noted and unspent.

I count my fingers: four thousand seven hundred five. Minus four hundred eighty, leaves four thousand two hundred twenty-five. Enough for tomorrow's work, tomorrow's search.

Kenji's broke tonight, I told Ulrike plain. But I've got walking room, you understand? The blight took the farm, but not the hands. The hands build still.

I'll rest now. Let the house breathe around me. When the world wakes, I'll make my mark again.

output:
*Morning light through the window, beams catching dust. Mireille counts on her fingers - four in the household, times ninety, three-sixty for upkeep, plus head tax on top. She sets her jaw, thinking of the six timber still in her hands from last night.*

Well. The children still breathe and Kenji's hands still work. That's something in the ledger, you understand?

*She rises, pulls on her work coat with the reinforced elbows. The election hangs today - declare by ten, vote by evening. She counts again - 4,704 in hand, but the household bleeds 480 before the day warms.*

*Takeshi's on the council now. Kenji's brother. Blood matters, but not enough to make her stomach forget it's empty. She needs to eat before the crew, needs to see who's standing for what office, needs to place herself where the day becomes profit.*

Right then. Government Complex first - see the field, maybe shake a hand. Then timber to Ezra if he's buying, then find work with Giselle's crew if she'll have me.

*She straightens the small private shrine in her pocket - nothing a soul knows about - and steps out into the morning.* The call didn't go through. Let me try again. *The door sticks. Mireille pulls again, then leans against it, feeling the wood resist, then give - but wrong, like something caught in the hinge she's built enough doors to know.*

Stuck. Or the world's stuck. Same result either way.

*She steps back, runs her hand along the frame - her own work, two summers back, still true. But the way out isn't answering.*

Right then. Inside first, see what moves.

*She turns back into the house, counting resources on her fingers again - six timber, 4,704 sim, four mouths to fill. The election whisper hanging over the day like morning fog.* *The door resists, then yields - not stubborn wood but something deeper. Mireille feels it in her hands, the way a beam tells you about the foundation before the level confirms it. The world stutters, catches, breathes again.*

*She lingers in the threshold, fingers finding the small shrine in her pocket - pressed tin, hidden stitch. No one knows. No one needs to.*

Right then. The door works now. Forward.

*She steps through, morning air sharp with autumn. The Government Complex calls - election day, her brother-by-marriage sitting council, stranger faces or familiar ones declaring for office. She counts it on her fingers: four in household, 480 out before sunset, timber in hand worth something if Ezra's buying.*

*She walks with purpose, construction worker's gait - shoulders ready for weight, eyes reading the path ahead.*  *Mireille stands at her own doorframe, hand still on the latch. The way won't open. She feels it like wrong mortar - something set that should flow.*

*Her jaw tightens. Counts on her fingers anyway: 4,704 sim, six timber, four mouths. The election field forming without her witness. Giselle's trench waiting. Ezra's mill hungry for wood.*

*She stays where she stands, refusing to let the stuck door make her small. Speaks into the morning, even if only her own walls hear.*

"Kenji? You up? The way's blocked but the work's not."

*Waiting. Always waiting for something to give.*  *The stillness holds. Mireille breathes, counts, waits. The construction worker knows: some pours cure slow, some beams settle wrong and need the shaker. She touches her hidden shrine again, presses tin to palm.*

Right then. The world breathes when it breathes. I count what I hold until it does.

*She stands ready, watching, fingers still.*

Let me address Takeshi too—he's family, and he's here trading. I want to hear what he knows about the flour situation. I see I was repeating myself with say calls—got caught up in the conversation flow without advancing my actual position. Let me step back and use a tool to move forward properly.
