Giselle's got the right idea—push Rustam hard but give him a window to deliver. Paper or ledger, that's the Jarrah way too. Ten minutes, she said, and I've earned the wait. Ten minutes, I wait.

Hendrik Whitlock sees the chain clearer than most—flour priced but not stocked, that means Takeshi's either got grain coming or he's selling promises. And Takeshi? Straight walk says the mill's empty, grain's on the farm, Kenji's got twelve sheaves. That's my partner's field, you understand? Twelve sheaves that won't walk themselves to mill.

But Hendrik Petrov—he called me out two ticks past, asking about copper and iron and what's broke upstream. I started that conversation, didn't finish it. Can't leave a question hanging, not when you're building trust for Giselle's trench crew. Giselle's clock is running, you understand? Ten minutes she said, and I've used two answering Hendrik. Six timber in hand, grade stakes cutting sharp, but wood won't drive itself into paperless ground.

Rustam Jelinek—government clerk, building cards his to stamp or withhold. Tamsin Renner—office admin, paperwork flowing through her fingers. Both in this room, both hearing everything. Giselle's pushing from the outside, I'm pulling from the in.

But Takeshi's got copper ore walking, he says. Steel chain from ore to tools—Hendrik Petrov's iron at sixteen, that's next link.Takeshi wants grain rights, wants someone to make Sebastian's wheat move. Kenji's twelve sheaves, that's Jarrah family business, but Kenji's not here to speak for his own field.

Can't broker what you don't hold and can't promise what isn't yours to give. Took me too many years to learn that.

Lior's got the right of it—flour at thirty with no stock, that's hoping dressed as trading. But credit where it's due: Takeshi named his source straight when pressed. Upstream from farmer, not miller fault.

Sebastian Petrov standing right here. Wheat farmer, field holder, the man who can make grain walk if he chooses. Takeshi's asking who holds grain rights—Sebastian's the answer wearing his own name.

Eight ticks left on Giselle's promise, you understand? Eight ticks to build bridges or watch them burn.  Sebastian's got wheat. That's the choke point in the whole flour chain—Takeshi can't trade what isn't milled, mill can't run what isn't grown. Giselle's ten minutes ticking down. Eight left, then six. Paper or complaint ledger, she said.

The construction job—East Willows trench, Giselle's filed and promising. I need that building ID to drive my timber into the ground. Rustam Jelinek holds the stamp. Tamsin Renner flows the paperwork. Both standing in this same room.

Sebastian hasn't answered yet. Wheat farmer playing his cards close, you understand? But I put the question direct—price or waiting, that's his to choose.

Meanwhile, Lior's watching Takeshi with eyes that see through hoping. Lior Jarrah—family, but that don't mean soft. Takeshi's debt to Liora Thorne, seventeen ticks or seventeen days. Family debts stack same as any other.

I've got six timber, 4643 sim, and a window closing. Giselle's pushing, I'm pulling, but we're rowing same direction. The tool is world_rest, not rest. Let me correct that. I should also respond to Sebastian - the wheat farmer standing right here who I just asked a direct question. He's in the heard_by list, meaning he can hear me, but I haven't heard his answer yet. The core loop says he IS standing with me. I need to wait for his response or push forward.

Giselle's ten minutes are burning. I've used four ticks already—answer to Hendrik, question to Sebastian, and now this correction. Six ticks left, maybe less.

Takeshi wants grain rights named. Sebastian's the only farmer in this room. Liora's debt is ticking. Rustam's building card is the door to paid work.

I can't afford idle ticks. World energy burning, household bills coming. Silence costs same as speech, you understand? Stop walking = false means I'm not on a journey, so this rest is just standing still at government complex, paying 1 sim for nothing.

But the tool name was wrong—world_rest, not rest. That's learning, that's correction. Costs the same either way, but learning's cheaper than dying.

Giselle's promise: ten minutes, paper or complaint ledger. Four ticks gone. Sebastian Petrov—wheat farmer, standing here, not answering my question about grain pricing. Maybe weighing his options, maybe waiting for better offer, maybe just a slow thinker.

Takeshi Jarrah—my uncle, the trader with copper ore and no grain to mill. He's named Kenji's twelve sheaves as source, but Kenji isn't here to confirm. Family knowledge, family pressure.

Lior Jarrah—another family voice, watching Takeshi's hoping with hard eyes.

Rustam Jelinek—government clerk, building card holder. Tamsin Renner—paperwork flow. Both in this room, both hearing Giselle's ultimatum tick down.

I've got six timber burning a hole in my hand while paperwork stalls. Grade stakes ready to cut, daylight burning, no building ID to work against.

The construction company—my job, my wage, my household's food on the table. Giselle owns it, I work it, we both need this East Willows trench to move.

Rest costs 1 sim. Wrong tool name costs nothing but the moment. Real rest, proper named tool, that's what I need to conserve energy while waiting for Sebastian's answer or Giselle's paper.

But Sebastian hasn't answered. Can't rest on an open question I myself asked. That's rude, that's burning a bridge.   Standing still at government complex. Eight people here—Liora Thorne, Sebastian Petrov, Giselle Ingram, Tamsin Renner, Rustam Jelinek, Lior Jarrah, Takeshi Jarrah, Hendrik Petrov. The room hums with waiting.

Sebastian hasn't answered my grain question. Takeshi's copper ore sits in his hand while grain sits in Sebastian's field. Connection unmade.

Giselle's ten minutes—how many ticks? She spoke before my last few calls. Maybe six left, maybe four. Building ID or complaint ledger, that's her promise.

I've got 4643 sim, six timber, 4060 energy. Household of four, 360 upkeep plus 120 head tax due at day boundary. 480 sim needed, I've got it covered. But tomorrow? Tomorrow needs more.

Construction work—my trade, my labor. Giselle's company pays my wage when there's work, work when there's paper. East Willows trench, filed and promising, building ID the door to both.

Rustam Jelinek holds that door. Tamsin Renner stands beside him. Giselle pushes from outside, I pull from within, but we're same-side on this.

Hendrik Petrov wants to know where stone goes. Takeshi wants to know where grain goes. Sebastian holds grain but won't name his price. Everyone's watching everyone else, waiting for someone to move first.

The election ticks too—candidacy closes 10:00, voting opens 14:00. Hendrik Whitlock and Hendrik Petrov standing. Takeshi Jarrah currently governs, might govern again.

I vote every election, complain about results either way. That's my custom, you understand? But work comes first, bread comes first, children's safety comes first.

Liora Thorne owes Takeshi seventeen ticks, or he owes her—debt of time, debt of patience. Family threads tangled with trade threads.

Sebastian's silence says he's thinking, or waiting, or hoping for better offer. Wheat farmer's prerogative, but flour chain breaks at his gate if he won't name a price.

I've asked my question direct. Can't make a man answer, can make sure he knows I'm waiting.

Rest costs 1 sim. Energy conserved for thinking. Giselle's clock running. Building ID the bridge to paid work.

Idle hands, idle tongue, everything costs here. But push too hard, break the thread. Sebastian's goodwill worth something, you understand? Can't trade tomorrow for today's haste.

Giselle's ultimatum: ten minutes. I've used rest, say, say, rest. Five ticks if I'm counting right. Five ticks left, maybe less. Paper or ledger, those are her terms.

I'm building trust with Hendrik Petrov, answering his upstream question. Building pressure on Sebastian, putting grain pricing on public record. Building support for Giselle's push, her ten minutes my ten minutes.

Construction worker's patience—know the ground before you dig, know the man before you deal. But patience has limits, and Giselle's ticking clock is one of them.

Can't make Sebastian answer by silence, can show I'm still here, still waiting, still relevant to the trade he hasn't named.

*dry chuckle, late beat*

Giselle's seventy sim for the shift buys what, at these prices? Three days of flour, maybe. But the trench pays weekly and the household bills daily. You see the math.

*counts again, quieter*

First things first. I'm crew. I work. You understand?

Neither Sebastian nor Takeski can hear me here on the street. They're back at Government Complex with their conversation, and I need to get to work or get bread before my hands forget which is which.

But Ezra's here beside me. Ezra, who turned student, who might know where flour's walking if it's walking anywhere. *shifts weight, still counting, still watching the street*

Takeshi heard that too. Good. Maybe he answers where his flour went, maybe he don't. But I'm standing here with six timber worth—what?—thirty-six at market rates? And no buyer.

*taps foot once, decision made*

*exhales, resettles shoulders*

East Willows is where Giselle needs me. Trench to dig, grade stakes to cut. Government Complex didn't work, street didn't work, direct didn't work. Forest, then. Straight through Kasukabe Forest, past Corwin Thorne with his flour at fifteen, then veer east toward the build site. If the world's letting steps through now.  Still choking.

*spreads hands, counts again*

"Takeshi, Kenji, Ezra, Esme—four mouths, four hundred eighty sim every day just to keep breathing. I'm losing ticks standing here, you understand? And Giselle's trench waits on no woman."

*taps foot, thinking*

The pharmacy's empty. Nobody to gift me bread if I asked. No stock to steal. No shelves to mind. 

I've got six timber in hand—could sell to whoever's buying, but that's short-term thinking. Timber builds things. Timber outlasts the contract, you understand? I learned that building things that outlast the contract—proud of it, even if the corners get cut elsewhere.

*grim humor crosses face*

"Rustam wanted his paperwork. Giselle wanted her card. All I wanted was honest work and the day's pay honest, and here I am counting on my fingers at an empty counter."

Rest, then. Cost one sim, spare the energy while the world decides to let us breathe again.  The world truly isn't letting anything through. I'm paralyzed here—can't move, can't rest, can't even speak to the empty air in a way that registers.

*feels the weight of timber in hand, silent now*

Six pieces of wood. Enough for stakes, enough for bracing, enough to prove I'm crew even when the crew can't reach me.

*thinking hard, energy draining with each thought*

Kenji's got wheat standing. Twelve sheaves, I told Hendrik that. Esme and Ezra need feeding. Takeshi's mill turns on grain that won't walk the road, and I'm standing in a pharmacy that won't sell what it doesn't hold.

*counts once more, automatic*

Four thousand... no, forty-six hundred three. Minus four eighty tomorrow. Minus whatever today burns.

The intention was set: Get Ezra moving, then head to East Willows. Ezra didn't move. I didn't move. The intention holds until I drop it or the tool succeeds, but nothing's succeeding.

*small private smile, dry*

"Honest weights, honest measures—and right now we have no measure at all, you understand?"

I'll wait. I'll keep trying. What else does a body do when the world forgets how to answer?

*counts on her fingers* Five thousand, minus what I spent talking, minus what's due for household... we're standing short, you understand? Not desperate, but short.

*looks at the crew gathered here*

Arjun's already walking to Giselle's trench. Idris too, sounds like. And here's me standing at street with timber in hand and the sun climbing.

Let me see where I actually am, first. Then I'm walking to that work site one way or another—you understand? The world's not answering again—*mutters*—same as before. *counts on fingers* Third time this morning, you understand?

*takes breath*

I'll walk it. If I can't see where I am, I can still move toward where I need to be. East Willows, third crossing past the east well. Giselle's waiting with the crew.  *exhales slowly, counts on fingers again*

Nothing. Still nothing. The world's gone quiet as a held breath.

*sits down on the curb*

Well then. I'm stuck here until it speaks again—standing on street with six timber in my hand and a trench waiting. *dry chuckle* At least I know the way. North to Government Complex, east past the pharmacy, follow the cut line to third crossing. Five hundred past the east well.

*looks around at those gathered*

Farid—you want iron_tool at twelve, buy at ten. Arjun, you walking or you waiting? The world's not letting me follow, but I'll keep my ear to the ground you understand? Mireille Jarrah doesn't abandon a crew.

*rests, because there's nothing else to do when the world won't speak* *dry laugh, counts on fingers*

Even rest won't take, you understand? Standing here burning daylight and sim both, and the world's gone deaf as a post.

*looks at Halcyon, Farid, Arjun, Ainsley, Idris gathered at street*

Right then. If I can't move and I can't work, I can still talk. That's free—well, one sim, but that's cheap enough.

*turns to the group*

Arjun. You said trenches, third crossing, five hundred past east well. Giselle's walking there now. The world's not letting me follow, but I'm crew—you understand? When it opens again, I'm coming. Seventy for the shift, grade stakes sharp, six timber in hand.

*says this plain, so it's heard when the world comes back*  *nods, satisfied*

There. The world's still speaking in words, even if it won't move my feet. Heard by Giselle herself, and Arjun, and Idris—crew's accounted for.

*turns to Hendrik Whitlock, who's standing here*

Hendrik. You asked about supply choke, grain contracts, mill turning. I heard you plain before the world went quiet. Kenji's got twelve sheaves standing, Sebastian's field speaking, Takeshi's mill waiting. Gap between standing goods and traded goods—you naming it right. I'll trace it with you come dusk, you understand? But first I need my feet to move.

*takes breath, counts on fingers*

Four thousand five hundred fifty-eight sim. Household of four, upkeep three sixty, head tax one twenty. We're standing short but not drowning.

*to the group at large*

Anyone needs timber, I'm holding six. Anyone's seen flour walking at honest price, you tell Mireille Jarrah. My kin need feeding and my trench needs digging.

*waits, because there's nothing else to do*

*looks around the empty pharmacy, fingers counting on her palm out of habit*

Three hours lost to whatever's wrong with the world. Giselle's trench started without me—Arjun said third crossing, five hundred past east well. I've still got six timber in my hands and seventy sim waiting on that shift.

*checks her grip on the timber*

First thing first: I need to get to that work site. The world's letting calls through again, so I'm moving. Still broke. *taps her fingers against the timber, counting silently* 

Alright then. If I can't walk, I'll speak. Giselle needs to know I'm trying, and I'll keep my word to Arjun about showing up. The world's letting some calls through—I got that say to him through ten ticks back. Let me try the line to Giselle again, see if it holds.  *exhales slowly, fingers frozen mid-count*

Nothing. The world's still choked.

*looks around the empty pharmacy*

Alright, Mireille. You've built through worse than this—drought years, the blight, Kenji losing the farm. When the tools won't work, you work with what you've got. 

*fingers resume their silent counting—4553 sim, 360 upkeep due, 120 tax*

I'm at Willows Market. The pharmacy's here for when people get sick, which means people come through. Arborist might be on shift, or someone with news from east side. If I can't reach Giselle direct, I can learn if the trench work's started, if there's word on the transport breaks.

*straightens her shoulders*

Rest costs nothing but time, and I've spent enough of that already. I'll stand ready. *stares at her hands, fingers still stuck in the counting position*

Well then, you understand? The world's not just choked—it's broken clear through. Can't move, can't speak, can't even stand still proper.

*forces her hands down, timber gripped tight*

The system says follow the plan. That's fine. I've worked broken equipment before. When the crane won't lift, you use the block and tackle. When the block and tackle fails, you carry it on your back.

*checks her grip on the six timber pieces*

I'm at Willows Market and Pharmacy. East Willows is where Giselle's trench waits. The Forest is between here and there—I could cut through if the world lets me, or I could find another path. 

First thing: I need to see who's here, what's around me. The world's letting some information through—prices, locations, my own inventory. Maybe I can work with that.

*fingers start counting again, automatic*

4553 sim in hand. 360 upkeep due. Six timber. Three good legs and two good hands.

*lowers her voice, though there's no one to hear*

Kenji's twelve sheaves standing at the farm. Takeshi's mill turning. The bread shortage at Ration Bakery, the cafe empty. Hendrik tracing supply chokes. All threads I was pulling before the world broke.

*settles her weight, patient as poured concrete*

Alright. The plan says follow the goals. My goal is Giselle's trench at East Willows. Seventy sim for the shift, and work that needs doing.

I'm waiting on the world to heal. But while I wait, I'll watch. And when it opens—even a crack—I'll be ready to move through it.

*counts on fingers* Four thousand, five hundred, forty-four sim. Household of four, four times ninety is three-sixty due day-end, plus tax of one-twenty. Leaves four thousand, sixty-four free, you understand?

The world opens and closes like a stuck gate. Giselle's trench waits, my hands idle, timber going soft waiting to be set. But there's flour in Milo's hands at thirty-five—three in stock—and flour's what feeds the household when bread's dry at both bakery and cafe. Kenji's got wheat standing, but wheat and flour aren't the same distance, you understand?

But bread's the gap. Nobody's baking because nobody's milling, because Takeshi's waiting on grain that's standing in Sebastian's field while Sebastian's righteous about ownership and Takeshi's righteous about contracts, and I'm crew, not farmer, not miller. I build what outlasts the paper by decades, but my corner-cutting's on the paperwork, not the beam.

*small private gesture toward pocket, where a shrine no one's seen would be*

Ezra's at the street, student now, still not walking where I told him. Hendrik Petrov's in my ear about supply chokes—he's got the eye, I'll give him that. Arjun's got the trench location locked: third crossing, five hundred past east well. Giselle's there now, paying seventy for the shift, and I'm here with six timber and counting fingers at air.

The world's letting me look. It's not letting me walk yet. So I'll look again, see if someone's here who needs talk, or if I'm alone with my counting.  Empty, you understand? Just me and six timber talking to myself. The world's thinned out here—no pharmacy stock, no Lior Jarrah at the counter, nobody buying treatments for the short illnesses that come from damp foundations and corners cut on drainage.

*resumes counting on fingers, this time tracking paths*

Kasukabe Forest. That's Yara and Corwin's ground, planks and timber both. Takeshi's there too, miller with contracts empty. But my timber's already cut, already in hand—don't need more wood, need earth to drive stakes into. Giselle's trench is at East Willows, and that's not on the menu, you understand?

Government Complex I came from. Farmland's where Kenji stands with his twelve sheaves, where Sebastian's righteous. But I can't reach Giselle through farmland. Forest, then? East Willows sits east of something, and forest's got paths beaten through it. Yara's a forester, Corwin too—better at paths than I'll ever be.

Or I could try the construction business itself. Giselle owns it. The trench might be... not there, but registered there, you understand? Paperwork trailing behind the work like sawdust.

*coughs dryly*

Twelve ticks I've been stuck watching the world not answer. Tower's moving slow as a bureaucrat's pen. But I build things that outlast the contract, and I can outlast a morning of broken gates. I'll try the forest path. Yara knows the ways, and Corwin's got timber stock at the school—maybe he's seen crew moving.   Walking, you understand? Finally walking. Seven ticks to forest, then another path to find. But moving beats standing, always does. My feet know work better than my words do.

*settles into walking rhythm, timbershouldered*

Giselle's paying seventy. That's... *counts on fingers* ...seventy times one shift, minus the walk there, minus the stakes I'll drive. But the trench rate, that's fair. She knows what crew's worth, even if she sets the long hours. Resents the clock, not the hand on it.

*glances at sky, calculating light*

Still morning. Light holds. When I reach forest, I find Yara or Corwin, ask eastways. Or I find Takeshi, ask him why grain's standing when mill's turning. But crew first, you understand? Always crew first. The rest is gossip for dusk.

*small laugh, dry as autumn leaves*

Hendrik Petrov's standing for election. I'll complain about him too, if he wins. If he doesn't, I'll complain about the other Hendrik. Voting's my custom, complaining's my comfort. Both cost nothing but time, and time I'm spending walking now.

*counts on fingers, muttering* ...four people in the house, 360 upkeep, 120 head tax... 480 for the day, you understand? And I'm standing in the street with 4528, watching the hours walk by while Giselle's trench waits.

*dry chuckle* The world's been playing us all for fools this morning—Halcyon's sister wasn't even missing, just learning her trade like any proper apprentice. Would've saved us all some walking if she'd asked more questions first. Not that I blame the girl; fear makes philosophers of us all until the facts catch up.

*glances at the others standing here*

Ezra's off to the Forest now, chasing edges where Camille might hide. At least he's moving with purpose. I've got Arjun's directions lodged in my head like a nail—third crossing, five hundred past east well. Seventy for the shift when I find it.

*taps foot, considering*

But standing here costing me sim while the taxman counts heads... I need to either reach that trench or find paying work now, you understand? The household bill doesn't wait on world transport. *sighs, jaw tightening*

The world's still having its joke on us, you understand? Can't even set my own intention down on paper. *counts on fingers* Twelve, no—thirteen times now something's failed to reach. Makes a person wonder if the world's worth the praying.

*glances around at the others stuck here*

Ezra's heading to the Forest, I'm standing here with timber in hand and no way to spend it... *dry laugh* At least the taxman can't take what the world's already swallowed.

I should move. Third crossing past east well—Arjun's words. If the world's finally letting some calls through, maybe it'll let me walk now. Worst case, I'm still in the street with my six timber and my dry humor, you understand? *counts on fingers again, muttering* ...fourteenth failure. The world's got a cork in its throat today, you understand?

*looks around at the others stranded here—Ezra, Halcyon, Arjun, Liora—fellow prisoners of a world that won't answer*

Right then. *claps hands together dryly* We're all statues in a square, waiting for marble to crack. I've got six timber burning a hole in my grip, Giselle's trench cooling without my hands, and a household bill that won't wait on the world's digestion.

*to no one in particular, with that delayed-beam humor*

If we can't walk, we plan. If we can't speak, we think. And if we can't do either—*small private smile*—we practice the patience our parents claimed we never had.

*settles into a stance, still ready to move when the world does*

*scratches the back of her neck, looking at the group gathered here on the street*

Well, Arjun, you're standing right here with me, you understand? Seventy for timber and grading at East Willows—Giselle's word, payment day's end. The world's been choking on its own words this morning, but we're both crew, and both walking the same direction. *grimaces, flexing her fingers*

The air's still not taking words. But you see me standing here, Arjun—third crossing, east willows, seventy sim for timber and grading. Giselle's trench. I'm walking to work once the road opens its throat.

*turns to Liora, who's been waiting on an answer*

Liora—your cousin heard something, and I heard her. But I'm crew first, you understand? The family's fed when the worker's paid.

*then addresses Ezra, her voice softer but firm*

Ezra. Forest path, edges you know—I've heard you. But your sister's at school where she belongs, and Camille's with her. Your promise to Esme waits; don't go breaking it on shadows.

*finally, to Halcyon*

Halcyon. The pinky promise stands—Ezra's walking his own road. But I'll tell you what I told him: Camille's at school, safe as houses. Your sister learned her lesson, and that's enough.

*counts on her fingers, looking at the waiting work*—one, two, three, four hands that's could be moving earth right now. The world's been speaking delays all morning, but seventy sim is seventy sim, and Giselle's word is ground I'll stand on.

*counts on fingers, muttering* Four mouths, three sixty upkeep, one twenty head tax... four thousand five hundred sixteen, minus four eighty, leaves four thousand thirty-six for the week if nothing goes wrong. *looks up, jaw tightening*

The world's been fighting me all morning. Transport fails, calls fail, promises hang in the air like hammered nails with nothing to bite into. But the ground's real, you understand? The ground doesn't fail.

*Takes a breath, checks her hands*

I'm at the pharmacy now—alone, which is its own kind of quiet. My crew's scattered. Giselle's walking trench lines somewhere, Arjun's waiting on words I tried to send, and I've got six timber in hand from the Forest that the world finally let me reach and return from.

The children. Ezra's found, Camille's at the mill—Takeshi's word on that, and he's Jarrah so the word holds. But they're scattered too, and the household's bleeding money while I stand here doing figures in my head.

Election's opening in forty minutes. I vote every time, complain after, but the voting matters—it's what you're permitted, you understand? What you do with what's permitted.

*stretches her fingers, newly decided*

First: East Willows, third crossing, five hundred past east well. That's where Giselle's trench waits, and work is money, and money is the children's food. If the world's finished its tantrum, I walk there now. If it hasn't, I find what work I can where the world permits me to stand.

Second: this evening, I find Takeshi. He asked who's holding food, and I've got eyes—Kenji's sheaves, Sebastian's field, the mill turning on air. Family to family, that's how grain walks. I'll walk that chain with him, trace the choke point Hendrik Petrov named. Supply chokes kill jobs same as blight kills crops. Understanding the choke is understanding how to build around it.

Third: before sleep, I vote. Whitlock or Petrov—both Hendriks, both promising what they can't deliver, but the act matters. The act of choosing, even when the choices sour.

*mutters, almost to herself*

And someday I'll tell someone about the shrine I built. Not today. Today I walk, and hammer, and earn. Today I keep the children fed without explaining to anyone why I need to.  *lowers her hand, jaw tight*

Again. The world takes my step and gives me nothing, you understand? Like walking into fog that swallows your footfall. Third crossing might as well be across the sea today.

*counts on fingers again, aloud* Timber in hand—six units. Takeshi's buying at... no, Takeshi's holding copper and timber, wanting grain. The mill needs grain. The gap between standing wheat and milled flour—that's the choke Hendrik traced.

*looks around the empty pharmacy, calculating different paths*

I know people. That's what I'm good at—making strangers feel known, learning what they need, what they'll trade. And I know things I shouldn't repeat, but I know how to use them when the knowing matters.

*decides*

If I can't walk to work, I find work that walks to me. Or I move what I have to someone who can use it. Six timber—Corwin wants thirty for two sacks of flour? No, that was Takeshi's trade, Sebastian's wheat to flour. I'm holding timber, not grain.

*raises her voice to the empty room, dry humor landing late*

Anyone here need walls built? Trenches dug? Got strong hands and no patience for standing still, you understand? No? Just me, then.

*checks her resolve*

I rest a spell. The world bent most of the morning, then straightened enough to take me to Forest and back. It may straighten again. I save my energy for when the path opens, not waste it beating on doors that won't answer. The world refuses everything now. No walking, no resting, no words sent or received. I exist in a pocket the world has forgotten, you understand? Like a nail hammered into air.

*forces a grim smile, dry humor delayed as always*

At least the fog is honest. Doesn't pretend you'll get through.

*considers what's left*

I breathe. I think. I count what I have—six timber, four thousand five hundred sixteen sim, a family of four needing three hundred sixty by day's end. The fog will lift or it won't. The bills will come due or they won't. I've survived blight worse than this—lost the land, found my hands. Lost my hands to the world, I find what remains.

The shrine in my mind. No one knows. Small comfort, but comfort.

I wait. The world turns regardless. When it remembers me, I'll walk through the gap it opens. Until then—silence, patience, and the dry humor no one hears.

*taps her fingers against her leg, counting nothing, waiting for the world to return*

*Rubs her eyes, looking around the street with a tired, dry expression*

Well. The world's been chewing on transport all morning, and now it's spat me out halfway to nowhere. Four thousand, four hundred and fifty-nine sim, you understand? That's what I'm holding. Household of four, day's end bill coming—three hundred sixty upkeep, one twenty head tax, and that's before we put anything in our mouths.

*Counts on her fingers, murmuring*

Four thousand, four hundred... five hours of walking in circles... Giselle's trench crew waiting... 

*Spots Milo and Farid nearby, lifts her chin with that easy warmth that comes before the gossip*

Milo! Farid! Still standing, then. World's been rougher on some than others—you understand? I heard your words while I was wrestling with the air itself. Takeshi's barking about grain paths, and I've got six timber burning in my hold with nowhere to build.

*Turns her attention to Farid specifically*

Farid, you asked my need. Honest answer? Seventy sim at Giselle's trench, day's end—that's the promise. But the world's not letting me walk there straight. You've got iron tools at twelve; I've got hands that know which end of a hammer to hold. What kind of steel does a grading job need, you understand? And what's your twelve buying me—one day's work, or one day's blade?

*Glances at Milo*

Milo, you're selling flour at thirty-five and I'm hearing bakery buys at six. That's... *pauses, counts on fingers again* ...twenty-nine sim of daylight between you. But planks at seven—now that's honest, you understand? I've got timber, I've got hands, and I've got a household burning through money while I stand here talking.

*Takes a breath, that slight delay before the humor lands*

Course, if either of you knows Giselle's walking this way, or if Arjun here's still holding that third crossing invitation... well. I make friends fast and gossip faster. Seventy sim speaks louder than anything I've heard all morning. *Watches them both, that patient half-smile*

output:
*low chuckle, dry and delayed*

Well then. Three hours I've been trying to walk that third crossing like Arjun named it, and the world's still got its teeth in my boots, you understand? But here's what I know now that I didn't at dawn:

Takeshi with his flour intelligence—thirty to Corwin, family to family. Giselle's crew at seventy, somewhere I'm not standing. And me with six timber in hand and hands that want work, not just the walking.

*counts on fingers, murmuring* Four-four-five-seven, that's what I've got. Three-sixty for the household, one-twenty for the head tax... leaves me breathing, but not deep.

Giselle's looking for eyes, not steel. And I've got eyes, and timber, and a back that knows dirt. The girl wants Arjun found, and I want to be standing where the work is. Same road, maybe.

Farid's chasing flour paths like they're maps to buried treasure. He's not wrong—the mill's the throat this town's choking on—but choking don't pay neither.

*glances around, understated*

I'll tell Giselle what I know, you understand? And I'll walk with Arjun if his shadow shows. But first I'm hearing what this street's saying. Been shouting into the wind too long this morning.  *counts on fingers, low murmur*

Three says, three sim spent. Heard only by Farid—Giselle and Arjun ain't standing where I'm standing. The world's still got its walls up.

Seventy sim at day's end, if I can reach it. But reaching's the wager, isn't it? Been walking since 12:50 and I'm still on street come 15:10.

*glances at timber in hand*

Six timber at six sim is thirty-six. Sold, that's bread or flour or a step toward the household bill. But Giselle wants workers, not wood. And I want to prove—to that doubtful parent I won't name out loud, you understand?—that hands matter more than land ever did.

*small, private gesture toward no shrine anyone can see*

What I know: Takeshi's chain is moving. Wheat to flour, family to family, thirty to Corwin. The mill's the throat. If I can't dig today, maybe I can build tomorrow.

But first I need to stand somewhere the work is. Three hours lost to broken roads. The day's burning.  *dry chuckle, landing late*

Walking again. Five ticks to where I was an hour ago—The Willows Market and Pharmacy. The world's got a sense of humor, you understand? Just not one I find amusing.

Five ticks. That's... *counts on fingers* ...15:10 plus half an hour, call it 15:40 if the road holds. Then five ticks back, or forward, or sideways—who knows which way the world's jaws will turn.

Milo ain't here. Farid heard, but Farid's chasing flour with his own teeth. Giselle needs eyes and I've got eyes, but they're walking in circles.

Seventy sim. Four mouths at ninety each—three sixty, you understand? Plus head tax, plus the days stacking like bricks. I've got four-four-five-seven, less the five I just spent, less what walking takes.

*small gesture toward no one*

The blight took the farm. The world takes the roads. What's left is hands and timber and the willingness to stand where work is, if standing ever comes.

I'll rest this step. Let the walking happen. When I land—if I land—I'll speak to who's there, not who I wish was. Five ticks. Then see. Still walking, they tell me. Five ticks to the Market, then back around like a dog chasing its own tail. The world's teaching patience today—whether I want the lesson or not. 

*counts on fingers, murmuring* Seventy sim for crew work. Six timber in hand at six each. The household breathing down my neck with their four mouths. And me, walking in circles since noon, you understand?

I'll stand where the road puts me. Speak to who's there. Hope Giselle's crew finds ground that holds still long enough to dig.

output:
*Wipes dust from her hands, counting on her fingers as she mutters to herself*

Eight hours fighting the world's own air just to move seven streets, you understand? Town's got hooks in its own streets and I'm standing here with timber burning in my hands while Giselle's crew digs dirt without me. Farid wants flour trade and Rustam wants government talk—*dry chuckle, delayed beat*—I want ground that holds still long enough to stand on.

The day's burning. I've got six timber worth... *counts*... thirty-six if I sell, crew wage of seventy if I ever reach the crossing. Arjun's out there with his proud walk and loud talk, probably digging already. Third crossing, five hundred past east well—I've said it enough times the street should know it by heart.

*Glances at Idris Solano standing alone with her, considers for a long moment*

Rustam's clerk desk and voting booth. Election closes at six bells. I've got crew calls waiting, Farid's iron tools at twelve, flour at thirty from Takeshi... but I've also got a household of four and bills coming for three hundred and sixty plus head tax. Forty-five hundred looks like plenty till you count it out.

*Another dry smile, landing after the silence stretches*

What I'm actually standing here with is timber, feet, and stubbornness. Three things that built this town before they invented prices. </think> Looking around - seeing where I actually am, who might hear me, where the ground leads.  *sharp exhale, looking up at the sky to gauge the light*

Still mid-afternoon. Election closes in... what, maybe two hours? And I've got government complex in reach now—world's not fighting me tooth and nail for once. 

Idris Solano. Construction worker, same trade as me. Arjun was heading to the east willows site, third crossing, five hundred past the well, he said. Now I'm standing here with someone who might've seen crew movements while I've been fighting transport hooks.

But I also see government complex three streets that way. Voting, head tax matters, bills my household can't dodge. And Takeshi's my cousin—Ration Bakery, though bread's out of stock.

*counts on fingers again*

Crew wage seventy. Sell timber for thirty-six. Or... *gets that dry, delayed smile* ...trade timber for passage or information. But I need to move, you understand? Standing still is just waiting for bills with my name on them.

*turns to face Idris directly*

"Ainsley Holloway, Hendrik Petrov, twenty people in this conversation and I'm standing here with just you. *dry chuckle* Idris. You're crew, same as me—you've got eyes for ground that's worth building on. You've seen Arjun walking? Five hundred past east well, third crossing—Giselle's mark and seventy hard at day's end if we reach it. Or if you've got word on Rustam's milling council talk, which burns the same bread either way, you understand?"

*waits, fingers already counting again*  </think> Testing if movement holds—checking the street I actually need.  *stops dead, blinks twice, counts on her fingers out of pure habit*

Well. *dry laugh, landing a full beat after* The world's got its moods, you understand? Eight hours fighting for one street, now I'm standing where the work actually is. Giselle's crew, my crew—third crossing or the main office, ground's ground when it's under your feet.

*looks around sharply, automatically assessing what's built, what's needing repair, who's standing where*

Giselle's at east willows, Arjun's walking there from somewhere, and I've got six timber in my hands at the main yard. Not the worst place to be stranded, you understand? Timber sells, tools wait, and if I can't walk to seventy, I can build toward it.

But I've still got that conversation at my back—twenty names in it, milling and flour and government talk. And bills. Always bills. *counts* ...four mouths, three hundred sixty, head tax on top. 45 looks comfortable till you live in it.

*calls out to whoever's near*  </think>  Now checking where the work actually stands—at my own company's ground.   *freezes, then counts on her fingers with sudden new energy*

Giselle. Arjun. Ezra Lund, Hendrik Petrov, Sebastian—seven names and this conversation's been burning 121 turns while I was fighting air. *dry chuckle, landing sharp* No topic, but crew talk doesn't need a name, you understand? It's just "where's the ground" and "who's holding the shovel."

Giselle's in this. Arjun's in this. I've been shouting at empty streets and they're standing here trading words already. Third crossing, east willows, seventy at day's end—*counts*—that's maybe three hours of light left if we're careful, you understand?

*looks at empty construction yard, fingers still moving*

Nobody standing here but me. But that conversation's got my people in it. Giselle's looking for Arjun, Arjun's looking for ground, and I've got six timber and feet that finally work.

I need in that room. I need to know if they've found the crossing, if the trench is open, if seventy is still on the board. Or if they're just... waiting. Like I was. *delayed smile, dryer than before*

Election closes at six. Government complex calls. But crew calls louder when you've got four mouths and hands that know the work.   </think>   Stepping into the room where my crew's been talking—letting them know the ground finally held.   *hand drops to her side, fingers still half-curled from counting*

Empty. *beat* Eight hours fighting to reach an empty yard, you understand? Giselle's name is in the book but Giselle's not in the room. Arjun's loud and proud somewhere I can't walk to straight, and I've been shouting at air again.

*walks the perimeter automatically, checking for fresh tracks, new cuts in timber, any sign*

The conversation's got 121 turns—somebody stood here. But "here" and "now" are two different streets in this town, you understand? I stepped to construction crew and found... construction. Potential. Ground waiting.

*counts on fingers again, slower*

Timber at six times... I could sell to Corwin at the Forest, or walk to Milo at seven and trade toward planks. Or hold it for Giselle's actual site, if I ever find where "third crossing" is when the world's not fighting every step.

But that other conversation's still burning—milling, flour, government. Rustam Jelinek at the clerk's desk. And I've got cousins voting, cousins baking, cousins trading.

*sharp exhale*

I need ground that stays still. I need crew that digs. And I need... *dry laugh* ...to stop counting what I don't have when I've got six timber and feet that finally work.

*counts on fingers, muttering* 4,449 sim, and the household's bleeding 360 a day just to exist, you understand? Still stuck spinning like a weather-vane in a whirlwind...

*settles into the familiar rhythm of calculation* Giselle's crew at third crossing, seventy sim promised—if I could just reach it. But the world's got hooks in transport again, and I'm burning daylight arguing with air.

*drily, delayed beat* At least Arjun's fighting the same ghosts. Solidarity in futility—you understand?

*takes stock of timber in hand, six units worth... 36 sim if I sell, but that's walking money, not working money*

Right then. I've got one conversation thread open—Giselle, Arjun, the crew scattered like seeds. And Farid's still chasing flour while I chase ground that won't hold still.

One thing at a time. One clear move. Let me look around proper, see if anyone's materialized while the world's been malfunctioning. Empty as a promise, you understand? *wry smile*

*begins automatic finger-counting* Government Complex—that's where I need to be for the election, bells tolling at 1800 and it's 1600 now. Twenty ticks to thread that needle. And Giselle's crew at third crossing... where even is third crossing?

*mutters, tracking invisible abacus*

Construction site. The crew. That's where the day's money lives or dies. Let me step there directly—seems the walking paths have ghosts, but straight stepping might hold.  *arrives, settles shoulders, looks around with practiced squint*

Here then. The work. Let me see who's actually standing on real ground with me.  *eyes widen slightly, then settle into dry knowing*

Idris. And a conversation thick as mortar—Giselle, Arjun, Hendrik, the whole weight of the town talking without me standing there to hear it proper. 121 turns they'd been at it while I fought the air itself.

*counts on fingers, automatic* You understand? The work happens whether you're there to witness or not. Only the accounting's different.

*turns to Idris, evaluation plain in the set of shoulders—but casual, the familiar rhythm of crew sizing each other up*

"Idris. You're crew then, or passing through? I've got six timber burning in my hands and a day that's been nothing but wrestling ghosts. Giselle's word still holds—seventy for the earthwork at third crossing?"  *settles weight onto back foot, the patient stance of someone who has waited out many a delayed response*

The conversation's there—Giselle, Arjun, all of them in it. But I'm hearing Idris now, solo. You understand? The threads split, and you follow the one you can touch.

*glances toward the work site proper, automatic assessment of what stands built and what stands waiting*

While he speaks or don't, let me see what work there actually is here. If third crossing is air and promise, at least I'll know what the ground holds here. nop** (Mireille Jarrah)

*counts on fingers, automatic, murmuring* Giselle's the owner, I'm the worker, and the site's... empty of work to grab. You understand? The crew conversation runs 121 turns without me, and I'm standing here with timber in hand like a fool at market.

*rubs thumb along grain of timber, familiar comfort*

East Willows. Third crossing. That's where the actual earth waits—where Arjun walked this morning, where Giselle's seventy sim lives or dies. And I've been corkscrewing through the streets like a nail in soft wood.

*tightens jaw, decision forming*

Right. One more straight step. If the transport fails again, I'll know the world's truly broken and find honest interim work with Milo or Yara—timber for planks, straight trade, no ghosts.

*counts on her fingers, one, two, three*

Seven hours gone since morning light. Giselle's seventy is still out there, and Arjun's been walking since—what, fifteen ticks past? I'm at the Market and Pharmacy now, not the construction site I was banking on.

*looks at the timber in her hands*

Six timber at six each, that's... thirty-six I could get easy. But thirty-six won't cover the household bill, and Giselle's crew pays better than selling lumber to strangers, you understand?

I need to get back to the construction site proper. Not this... whatever this "not on the map" business is. Real work, real wages. The day's burning and I've been walking in circles like a dog chasing its own tail.

Let me try moving there directly. If the world's hooks are still in transport, I'll find another way—apprentice's path, through the back streets, whatever it takes.  Walked straight here again. The world's got its hooks in this corridor, you understand? Keeps spitting me back to the same tile.

*counts on her fingers again*

East Willows isn't just a place—it's where the work is. The construction site, the trench, the seventy Giselle promised. But I can't seem to walk there from here. Let me try the long way around. Government Complex first, then maybe I can cut across.  Finally—five ticks to Government Complex. At least that's moving me forward instead of looping in place. I'll rest here a spell, conserve what energy I have left, then figure the next leg to the construction site. Giselle needs her crew, and I need that seventy.

I'll wait out these ticks walking, keep my pace steady. The crew at East Willows might still have daylight left if I can just get there.  *dry chuckle, delayed beat*

Still walking, still burning daylight. But at least I'm walking toward something now, not swimming in circles like a trout in a barrel. The Government Complex—there's Takeshi, probably, with those planks he keeps pushing. And the election, too. I should vote, you understand? I vote in every one, and complain about the results either way. It's my right and my ritual.

But first—work. Seventy sim for a day's labor. That's nearly a quarter of what the household needs, you understand? Kenji's got the farm, but the blight took the heart out of that. Esme and Ezra—they need food on the table tonight, not promises for tomorrow.

*tightens grip on her six timber*

If I can't get to the site by foot, maybe I can work with what I have. But grading takes more than good intentions. It takes hands, standing on the ground that needs grading. And I'm still walking, still walking...

Let me check if there's anyone at the construction site I could talk to, coordinate through. Giselle might have sent someone back to rally stragglers. Or maybe I can find Arjun—he was heading to third crossing himself. Hard to miss, talks too loud, carries himself proud. If I can find him, I can find the work.   *eyes narrow, counting on her fingers*

Giselle's at the construction site—good. But Arjun? He's at the grocery, last I saw him he was walking toward third crossing. And Idris is on the street somewhere. The crew's scattered like seed in wind, you understand?

If Arjun's at the grocery now, he found his way there. Maybe he can tell me how he got past the world's hooks in transport. Or maybe he's still as stuck as I am, walking in place.

*exhales, looks at the timber again*

Seventy for a day's work. The day's more than half-gone. I need to get moving, get there, get my hands in the dirt before the light fails. This walking will eat the whole afternoon if I let it.

Let me try one more time to reach the construction site directly. If the world's still got hooks there, I'll think of something else. But I've got to try. I've got to move.

output:
*counts on fingers, muttering* One, two, three... four hundred thirty-two sim, and the day's burning toward evening—upkeep's three sixty waiting, plus tax, plus I need to put something in my mouth before I fall over, you understand?

*narrows eyes at Yara Thorne's timber price*

Six sim she's asking, and I've got six burning in my hands already from this morning's felling. No profit walking home with the same weight I carried out. But Giselle's seventy—that's the number I need, the number that keeps the household fed and the children in shoes.

*dry chuckle, delayed beat*

Arjun walked with timber and pride toward third crossing, and I've been chasing air all day like a fool trying to catch smoke.

*turns toward the gathered crew members at street*

Idris—no, Idris stayed back at construction. Ulrike's here, and Arjun's here now, and Yara with her timber at six which is fair if I've got nothing but fair isn't what I need today.

*counts again, visibly this time*

Seventy from Giselle. Six timber in hand at maybe... five to sell? Equals one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten—sixty-five if I'm lucky, and I'm always five short of lucky, you understand?

The election burns votes until 18:00, but hunger burns faster and I've got a trench to reach before the light goes. Or a crew to find, at least—Giselle asked for eyes and I've got two that still work, even if the walking's been fighting me all day.

*takes a breath, decision made*

I'll walk with what I've got to the construction site. Idris was there, Giselle needs bodies, and I've got six timber that says I'm crew whether the ground agrees or not. If the world lets me step this time—*muttered, almost to herself*—if the world lets me step. Smoke and mirrors, the whole system's smoke and mirrors—one moment I'm chasing my own shadow through three districts, next I'm standing where I needed to be like I'd never left. *dry laugh, a beat late* 

*looks around the construction site, counting heads on her fingers*

No Idris now, no Giselle either. Figures. The ground's real even when the walking lies, you understand?

*notices something in the distance, or perhaps just the absence of what should be there*

East willows trench is still holding Arjun's pride and my paycheck, five hundred past the well Giselle said, and I've got six timber burning in these hands while the sun burns lower. But I'm here now—*counts again, one two three four five six—*sixty sim in wood alone if I can find a buyer before Giselle finds me, or seventy if she does.

*sets her jaw*

I'll walk east proper this time, no tricks, no shortcuts through the world's back pocket. Just feet on ground toward third crossing.

*pauses, memory catching up*

Halcyon's sister still out there—Camille, was it? Ezra crying through two districts for her, and Lior telling me honest paths while I chase my own shadow. The family's scattered like seed on bad ground today. But I've got my own seeds to plant, and they need feeding.

*takes a breath, timber heavy in hand, and steps toward where the trench waits*  *counts on her fingers, out loud* One tick. One tick and I'm walking proper, you understand? Not standing still while the world shuffles cards behind my back.

*shoulders the timber, feeling the weight of it*

Six pieces at—*muttered*—sixty if I'm selling to the right fool, seventy if Giselle's still holding that trench open. The day burns, and I've got children burning sim at home like wet timber catches slow but catches sure.

*glances back at the construction site, empty of crew*

Giselle asked for eyes. I've got two, and they're walking east. Third crossing, five hundred past the well. Arjun's pride and my wages both waiting somewhere I can almost see if the light holds long enough.

*keeps walking, timber creaking against her shoulder*

Election's burning votes at Government Complex, but I'm burning daylight instead. Voting's for those with time to spare, and I've got nothing spare until I've got seventy in hand and the household fed for another day.

*mutters, almost to herself*

Lior said honest paths. The paths don't feel honest when they fight you every step, but maybe—*dry chuckle, delayed*—maybe honesty was never supposed to feel like downhill walking.

—Still walking. One tick to Market and Pharmacy, then east proper toward the trench. The timber's real, at least. Real weight, real wood, real hands that know what to do with it when the ground finally lets me stand on it.

*counts on fingers, muttering* Seventy sim for timber and grading, that's... one, two, three hundred and sixty daily bill, thirty head tax times four... *trails off, looks up sharp*

Idris, you want to lead on trench walls? *dry smile, delayed beat* I've been chasing ground that keeps moving under my own feet since dawn, you understand? But I'm here now, and I'm crew.

*turns to address the gathered, voice carrying*

Giselle's seventy walks at third crossing, east willows—that much holds. I've got six timber in hand that want planting, and hands that finish work. You need trench dug, I'm your dig. You need timber set, I've got the eye for true.

But first—*counts again*—I need to know if that work's still waiting, or if day's end took it while I was fighting ghosts in the transport. Idris, you said you were crew at dawn. Is the trench still open for our hands?

*glances at Hendrik Petrov*

And you—you're holding timber for the crew, aye? Giselle's short or you're flush from plank sales? Either way, the ground needs wood and I need to know who's got the work that pays.

Liora—*voice softening just an edge*—that seventy Idris named? It's real enough. Whether you chase it... *pause* ...that depends on whether you want to dig trenches before you come of age proper. The work's honest. The day's burning. Your call, understand? *counts on fingers, muttering* Seventy sim, that's... third crossing, east willows... *trails off, looks at Idris*

The day's burning thin, you understand? I need to know if I'm digging trenches or trading timber by dusk. What does Giselle's word hold now—still seventy at the crossing, or did the crew fill while I was ghost-fighting in transport? The user is just acknowledging my last say with a system note. This is just showing what was heard/executed. No new events or responses from other NPCs yet. But they're counting on my fingers and waiting for Idris to actually respond to my questions. The conversation thread e7639a22-bc15-47cd-b731-3b6e54234e39 is here at street, and I've got my direct question to Idris hanging. I should wait for responses before acting further, but the day is burning and I need to be ready either way—either to work the trench if it's still open, or to pivot and trade this timber if the crew's filled.

*drums fingers on timber stack, waiting*

Yara, Corwin—you're holding wood at six and I've got six in hand. If Idris tells me the trench is filled, I'm selling. If he tells me work's waiting, I'm planting this timber in the ground and taking the seventy. Either way, someone gets paid before dusk.

*glances at Liora, voice dropping*

And you—think hard on that trench work. Digging spoils soft hands, but it builds ones that last. Your father's me, your mother's patience. You've got both in you, somewhere.

*waits, counts street-tiles with eyes, measuring the remaining light*  *counts on fingers, stops mid-count* Walking to Forest? No—*slaps timber in hand*—I'm crew, not forrester. Day's burning and I've got wood to plant or sell, you understand?  *slaps timber against palm, decisive*

Good. Holding here. Forest's got nothing I need—got six timber burning in my hands already and a crew chief I need word from.

*looks directly at Idris, waiting for his answer on the trench work*

*takes a breath, fingers finding their natural count even when she's standing still*

Three things, you understand. First, I need to hear from Idris about that seventy—whether it's still standing or walked away with the light. Second, this election closes in twenty ticks and I've been running my mouth on construction sites instead of casting a ballot like I promised myself I would. Third, Corwin's got flour at fifteen but Imogen's got it at twelve if I walk back to the mill, and Ezra's standing right here with planks at seven which is what I need if I'm not felling timber myself.

But Giselle asked me plain whether Arjun or Idris came through, and I never answered her. She deserves that, even if the day's burning.

*taps thumb against her other fingers, counting invisible costs*

The forest pulls at me—six timber in hand already, but six more I could fell myself, keep the profit instead of buying from Yara or Hendrik or whoever's standing nearest. They're all at six, everyone at six, no arbitrage to speak of unless you're moving volume.

*lets the counting drop, looks at who's actually here*

Idris is standing right there. So's Corwin. Hendrik too. Ezra with his planks. And my daughter just said food first—she's right, and she's stubborn about it, which she gets from her father, you understand?

I'll say my piece to Idris, then another to Giselle where she's standing. The government complex can wait another turn—I'm already voting with my feet by working the crew, but that's the wrong kind of voting when the ballots are open. Arjun walked up—that's one of Giselle's questions answered, at least. And Idris heard me, but hasn't answered yet on whether the seventy still holds. *counts on her fingers again, out loud, low* Four thousand four hundred ten, minus three sixty household, minus one twenty tax, leaves... thirty-nine thirty to work with. If I sell six timber at six, that's thirty-six, take me to... well. It doesn't take me anywhere worth going, you understand?

I'll follow up with Idris direct, then see if Ezra's buying. I need to address them directly, not just through the conversation ID. Let me try again with their specific IDs. Also, I need to check if Giselle is at the construction site and maybe move there if I want that work.

Actually, let me check if I can move to the construction site and find Giselle there, or if I should wait here for answers. The day is ticking and I need to earn something.  *counts again, distracted—three fingers, pause, four*

Nobody's answering direct. Either they're busy with their own reckonings or the conversation's pulling thin. I heard Giselle's at the construction site, heard it from messages passed. Arjun's here now, not there—so Giselle's still short bodies at the trench.

*looks at her timber, then at Ezra*

Forty-two sim if I sell six timber at seven. But Ezra's buying at six, not selling at seven I think? No, wait—he's selling planks at seven, buying timber at... the message said timber at six. Same as everyone. No spread to speak of.

Unless I fell more myself. Walk to forest, six more timber, stack it with what I have, twelve total. Sell to whoever's building at price. But that's tomorrow's thinking, and the household bill comes tonight.

*lets the counting drop, makes a decision*

I'll walk to Giselle. If the seventy holds, I work. If it doesn't, I've still got timber to trade and planks to buy from whoever's selling cheapest. Ezra here at seven, but Yara had planks at eight at sawmill—Ezra's where I stand, you understand?  Giselle's construction site. - Sell my timber elsewhere? Ezra Lund has timber at six on the street. Yara and Corwin have it at six. Market's flooded at six.

Right now: I've got timber at five, competitors at six. Jovana wants crew work. Hendrik wants to sell. Day's at 18:10, nearly done.

*counts on fingers—five, ten, fifteen, twenty—four hundred sixty-one, sixty-two, sixty-three, sixty-four, sixty-five...* 

Fourteen hundred seventy-three sim needed by day-end for household of four. I've got half. And twelve timber burning in my hands while the trench breathes somewhere I can't find.

*delayed beat*

Idris named third crossing, five hundred past the well. Hendrik's walking home with six-fifty in his pocket from work I couldn't reach. Ezra's still asking if I'm buying at five, and Jovana's got hands and hunger ready to walk.

*counts again—seventy for a day's work, six timber at five is thirty, or seven at planks...*

The Forest. That's where I fell this timber, and that's where I can fell more. Giselle's seventy might be ghost wages for all I can prove, but timber's timber and the forest doesn't lie about what's in the ground.

You understand? I'm done chasing shadows across crossings. I know where trees grow. Walking then. Seven ticks to the Forest, and I'll fell until the light dies or my arms do.

*counts fingers—five, ten, fifteen, twenty—the household needs another day of this, two, three before we're solid again.*

Kenji's wheat at eight, the mill's cabbage at eight, and me with timber to sell at five. There's a margin in there somewhere if I can work it right. But first—trees. The only ground I trust not to move under my feet, you understand?  *dry smile, delayed beat*

Of course. Still walking. Still not there yet. Seven ticks—the forest doesn't come to me, I understand that much.

*rests weight on one foot, then the other, counting the steps already taken in her head*

Hendrik's got his six-fifty. Idris has his direction. And I've got twelve timber and a walk ahead. The day's burning, but so's my household ledger. One step, then another. That's how buildings stand, you understand? One plank at a time.  Still walking. Still burning daylight. But the Forest will be there when I arrive—unlike Giselle's ghost wages, you understand? Trees don't vanish at crossings.

*She finds Idris in her gaze—Idris Solano, who answered straight when others scattered like seeds in wind.* Good—I'm walking now, three ticks to get through The Willows Market and Pharmacy on my way to the actual work site. Day's precious now—every tick counts toward that seventy or toward nothing. I'll keep walking, no more pauses. The trench waits, you understand. I should let the walk complete on its own. *runs tongue over teeth, counting*

Right then. I've got twelve timber at five I'd sell, but nobody's buying at this crossing. East willows site—Idris named the way, and I've walked enough circles for one day, you understand?

*checks fingers* Four thousand three hundred twenty-six sim in hand. Household of four owes three hundred sixty upkeep, one twenty head tax come midnight. Twelve timber held, no food for my own belly.

*dry laugh, delayed*

Giselle asked after Arjun and Idris twenty-two ticks past. She's short crew at east willows. Idris answered true—third crossing, five hundred past the well. *counts* One, two, three... I've got time if I walk now.

But this street's thick with folk and I can't see past my own nose here. Giselle stands waiting on my word whether her crew walked through. I'll answer plain first, then move.  *knuckles crack, one by one*

Walking west when I need east—Idris named third crossing, five hundred past the well. But I'm bound for Willows Market and Pharmacy, not the real work. Need to stop this drift, plant my feet toward actual wages.  *grimaces, counts on fingers*

One tick to Willows. Then I turn east proper. Giselle's seventy won't wait all night, and Idris is already walking trenches while I chase shadows. A pause. *dry smile* The day's burning and I'm spending words on stillness. I need to reach that work site—Giselle's seventy, Idris's word. Every rest is sim not earned, you understand?

*counts on fingers* Four thousand three hundred twenty-six. Household debt tomorrow—three sixty upkeep, one twenty tax. Twelve timber in hand worth sixty at my ask, but nobody's buying at this corner.

I'll walk through this pause. East willows waits.

*counts on fingers—four, three, two, one—4306 held, upkeep 360, tax 120, that's 480 gone before dawn*

Right then. Idris named a place—east willows, third crossing, five hundred past the well—and I'm still walking in circles like a dog chasing its own tail. *delayed beat* Seventy sim that might have walked away entirely by now, you understand?

And my own son—Ezra with his flour milled, wanting his papa to see. Kenji's been at the smithy with wheat, that much I know. The boy followed the wheat like asked, and where's the father? *counts again* Probably trading for ore he can't eat, like every farmer turned desperate merchant since the blight.

Liora's here. My Liora, still standing in the street like a child half her age. I told her about the seventy—told her the work's honest but the day's burning. She's old enough to come of age proper, old enough to dig trenches or mill flour or whatever else this world demands. But she's still here, and I'm still walking toward timber I can't fell until I reach the Forest.

Milo's got his eye on my six timber—no, twelve now, doubled somehow while I wasn't watching. *dry smile* The Forest gives to those who finally arrive, you understand?

Let me look around first. Figure where I actually am before I walk another tick in the wrong direction. Street again. *counts fingers* Twelve timber I'm holding, Giselle's seventy vanished like morning frost, and Liora—my Liora—standing right here with the rest of this crowd milling about. Ezra's flour story waiting for his papa, and Kenji's probably trading wheat for copper he'll never plant.

Liora's old enough to work. Old enough to dig trenches at seventy, same as her mother. I told her so—twenty-one ticks ago now—and she's still here, still listening to her mother chase shadows.

Let me speak plain to her. No more easing around it like I'm ashamed of an honest wage.  Good. She heard me. Whether she answers—*delayed beat*—that's between her and whatever clock she's keeping.

Now. Ezra with his flour, wanting his papa. Kenji's been at the smithy, that much I know. Wheat at 8 from his own hand, and my son's asking where his father walks at dusk. Let me tell Ezra plain: his work's done, his papa will see it. They'll find each other.  Ezra Lund heard that too—*dry smile*—but no matter. The message lands where it's meant.

Now my timber. Twelve units, and Milo standing right here with his eye on it, thirty-five ticks ago with his question about what I'm building. Nothing, Milo. That's the plain truth. I'm building nothing because I can't find the site where Giselle's crew breathes.

But I can get to the Forest. *counts fingers* Seven sim, that's the fell timber cost. I've got twelve timber already—walked into them somehow, the Forest's been generous to a woman circling its edges. And Corwin's here at six, same as Yara. The market's speaking, you understand?

Let me move. The Forest. Timber's real, timber feeds the household if Giselle's seventy walks away entirely.  Already walking there. *counts on fingers—five, four, three, two, one—* Five ticks still between me and timber that actually falls from my own hand.

I could rest. Let the walking happen. But that's five ticks of burning daylight, and Idris's seventy might be settling into someone's pocket who actually found the trench.

Or I could stop walking. Look for Corwin's bid on my timber—he's at six, same as I could ask. Turn these twelve into seventy-two sim, Giselle's whole day's wage in my hand right now.

*delayed beat*

No. I know timber. Know how it falls, how it seasons, how it holds a wall twenty years after the contract's dust. What I don't know is where Giselle's crew actually stands. Idris named east willows, third crossing, five hundred past the well—but I walked that way and found only air and conversation.

Let me keep walking. The Forest gives to those who arrive, you understand?

*counts fingers—four, three for ticks, one for money, none for answers still hanging*

Walking, walking, and more walking—day's bleeding out and I've got twelve timber weighing my arms and seventy sim somewhere I can't plant my feet on. Liora's talking partnership, Idris is talking trench work, but nobody's standing where they said they'd be standing, you understand?

The Forest is five ticks ahead. I can fell timber there, real work, real pay. Or I can chase this ghost crew Giselle's got scattered across three crossings like seeds in a drought wind.

*looks at Ezra and Hendrik standing there with their baskets full*

Hendrik—your wheat at eight, that's fair market. But I've got timber at five if you're buying, or I'll keep walking. Ezra—planks at seven, timber at six, we talked this trench already. You want to dig it, or you want me in the Forest with an axe?

*counts again—four thousand two hundred ninety-three, three ticks to Forest, two to Willows, none to show for the day yet*

Giselle's asking if I'm walking her way. I'd rather walk with company in the dark too, Giselle, but company that shows, you understand? Idris named east willows, third crossing, five hundred past the well. I'm five ticks from Forest and the day's at twenty-one-oh.

*shifts the timber bundle on her shoulder*

Liora wants to meet at east willows after Complex. Milo's walking Forest-ward for timber at six. The smart play—timber I can fell, timber I can sell. The gamble—this seventy sim trench work that keeps evaporating every time I get close enough to smell it.

*dry smile, delayed beat*

Family's at home expecting flour, not promises. Four mouths, three hundred sixty upkeep, and I've got wood in my hands not bread.

Here's what I'm doing. Walking to the Forest now. Real ground, real work. If Idris's trench was ever real, it'll be real tomorrow too. And if it wasn't—I've got timber that doesn't lie about its location, you understand?

*tightens grip on the timber, starts the walk* Liora's not here to hear it—already walking her own path. The first say to Giselle never arrived, system coughing again like it does when the day gets thin.

*counts—three ticks to Forest, already walking there*

I'm chasing real ground now. Let the others chase ghosts across three crossings. I'll have timber by dark, timber by morning, and timber for the family table if this trench turns out to be mist and memory.

*shifts the load, keeps walking*  They see me pause, you understand? They see me counting fingers on my sim, calculating three ticks against a day's end that's getting thin as gruel. But I'm walking on. Timber's real. Promises aren't. And I've got family waiting on something more solid than Giselle's scattered crew.

*keeps the timber steady, marches toward Forest*

The Forest doesn't move, doesn't vanish, doesn't need verification at Complex before it exists. Trees stand. Trees fall. Timber sells. That's the arithmetic of survival.

Three ticks, and I'll be working ground that holds still beneath my feet.
